acceptance_criteria.statement: The page opens with the Card-Testing Weekend as an event with its figures, not with a definition of trust or security.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: the Card-Testing Weekend, the part thesis and the reading order.

posts.title: Never Touch the Card: Tokenization, Vaults and PCI Scope
posts.question: How do providers keep card numbers out of everyone's systems, including most of their own?

know: How PCI DSS scope is determined by the path a card number takes, and which self-assessment questionnaire follows from which integration at Stripe and at Adyen.
What a provider token is, what a vault is, and what Stripe and Adyen have each published about theirs.
How stored cards are moved between providers: import, export and forwarding.
believe: Choosing how card data is collected is a compliance decision first and a user-interface decision second.
A hosted card field reduces the merchant's scope without removing the merchant's page from the attack.
can_do: Given an integration, say whether card numbers reach the merchant's systems and which self-assessment questionnaire applies.
List what a merchant still owns after moving to hosted fields: the scripts on the payment page and a plan for moving stored cards.
Say, for a statement about either company's vault, whether it is documented or not public.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a merchant that uses hosted card fields and claims it has no remaining card-data risk, the reader names the remaining exposure and the control for it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A ticket seller collects cards through its provider's hosted fields (card inputs served inside the provider's iframe) and loads a tag manager and a chat widget on the same checkout page. It tells its board: 'We file SAQ A, the shortest PCI self-assessment, so card data is not our risk.' What is wrong with that statement, and what should the seller do?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The page around the iframe is still the seller's: a script on it can overlay or replace the card form and copy what is typed. Since 31 March 2025 SAQ A eligibility includes confirming the page is not susceptible to script attacks, by its own controls or the provider's confirmation. The seller should keep an inventory of the scripts on the payment page with a reason for each, restrict them with a content security policy, and remove the ones it does not need.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given three ways of collecting a card, the reader orders them by how much PCI scope the merchant keeps and names the questionnaire for each.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Three shops take cards: one redirects to the provider's hosted payment page; one embeds the provider's card fields in an iframe; one has its own form and posts the card number from its server to the provider's API. Order them by how much of the PCI standard the shop must answer for, and name the self-assessment form each would file.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Redirect and iframe fields: SAQ A, with the script condition applying to the iframe case and not to the redirect. Own form posting raw numbers: SAQ D, the full questionnaire, because the shop's systems handle card numbers.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every statement about how Stripe's or Adyen's vault works is a dated quotation or citation of the company's own page, or is marked as not public; the chapter says in plain words where the public record stops.

thesis.question: How do providers keep card numbers out of everyone's systems, including most of their own?
thesis.claim: Providers keep card numbers out by collecting them in a page or frame the provider serves, giving the merchant a token that works only with that provider, and confining the real numbers to a vault kept apart from the rest of the provider's own systems (Stripe documents one that shares no credentials with its other services); this moves PCI scope to the provider and leaves the merchant two things it still owns: the page that hosts the card fields, and stored cards it holds only as that provider's tokens.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a merchant filing SAQ A has handed card-data security to its provider entirely, and that its stored cards can follow it to another provider whenever it chooses.
thesis.so_what: The integration choice (redirect, hosted fields, encrypted own form, raw API) should be made as a compliance decision before it is made as a design decision, the payment page needs a script inventory even under SAQ A, and a merchant should know how its stored cards would leave a provider before it needs to move them.
thesis.how_why: PCI DSS applies to every system that stores, processes or transmits card numbers or can affect their security, so scope follows the data path. A field served from the provider's domain takes the merchant's servers off that path; the page that embeds it stays on it, which is why the SAQ A revised from 31 March 2025 asks merchants to confirm their page cannot be used for a script attack. On the provider's side, Stripe's security page (n.d., accessed November 2026) describes a card data vault in separate hosting that shares no credentials with its other services, with AES-256 encryption and keys on separate machines; Adyen names the Adyen Vault and regional storage and publishes no comparable description. Neither publishes a vault design, and the chapter stops there. Two documented differences remain: Adyen accepts card data encrypted in the browser and passed through the merchant's server as SAQ A, where Stripe's own-form paths mean SAQ A-EP or D; and Stripe documents an export of card data to another Level 1 processor, while Adyen's help center lists an export article whose procedure could not be read in November 2026. A token is an identifier in the provider's database, so moving stored cards is a provider-to-provider transfer that takes weeks, not an API call.

role.contribution: Establishes the first relocation, of card numbers and PCI scope to the provider, and the vocabulary (scope, hosted field, provider token, vault) that the next three chapters build on.

transition_in.carries_over: The part's claim that a control moves data or liability and leaves a remainder, and the Card-Testing Weekend, in which Larkfield held no card numbers.
transition_in.introduces: The first and oldest case of the claim: moving the card number itself out of the merchant's systems, and what stays behind.

posts.title: The Card Number's Replacement: Network Tokens and Credential Lifecycle
posts.question: What is a network token, who issues it, and why are networks pushing every stored card toward one?

know: What a network token is, how it differs from a provider token, and the roles of token requestor and token service provider.
What a cryptogram is and what happens to a token when the card behind it is reissued.
What Visa, Mastercard, Stripe and Adyen have each claimed about approval rates and fraud, with dates, and what those figures do and do not measure.
How Stripe and Adyen each expose network tokens, as documented in November 2026.
believe: A stored card now has several representations, and the provider, not the merchant, chooses which one is sent on each attempt.
Published token uplift figures are vendor comparisons and cannot be compared with one another.
can_do: Explain why a membership keeps renewing after the member's card is replaced, and what the merchant's own record may no longer show correctly.
Question an uplift figure before using it in a business case.
Say which party requested a token and why that matters when changing providers, and where the public record does not answer.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a stored card whose underlying card is reissued, the reader says what happens to the next charge and what the merchant's records should and should not assume.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A streaming service stores cards with one provider, which has network tokens (substitute card numbers issued by the card network) switched on. A subscriber's bank replaces her card with a new number. What happens to next month's charge, and what should the service's own customer record assume about the card?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The network updates what the token points to, so the token keeps working without the subscriber doing anything. The provider decides per attempt whether to send the token or the card number and may retry with the other. The service should keep the provider's token as its key, expect the last four digits and expiry it displays to go stale unless it listens for update events, and not assume which credential was used.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a quoted uplift figure for network tokens, the reader says what kind of evidence it is and what to ask before relying on it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A sales deck says: 'Network tokens lift approval rates by 6%.' What would you want to know before putting that number into a business case?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Who measured it, on what traffic, against what baseline. The published figures are vendors' own comparisons of tokenized with non-tokenized volume, not controlled experiments: Visa's 2024 release says a six-basis-point increase while a secondary source attributes about six percent to Visa; Adyen reports 3% on average; Stripe reports 3.8% for a bundle that includes other features. They are not comparable, so the reader would measure on its own traffic.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Network fee amounts are attributed in the sentence to the processor bulletins or consultancy they come from, and the chapter says that the networks' fee schedules are not public.

thesis.question: What is a network token, who issues it, and why are networks pushing every stored card toward one?
thesis.claim: A network token is a substitute card number that the card network issues for one card at one merchant or device, at the request of a merchant, provider or wallet, and maps back to the real card during authorization; the networks push stored cards toward it with stated targets and with fees on untokenized transactions, and the effect of that push is to make the network, instead of each merchant's or provider's vault, the place where a stored credential is kept valid, restricted and priced.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a network token is a security upgrade with a free approval-rate gain, which a merchant switches on once and can then forget.
thesis.so_what: A merchant should treat the provider token as its record key and never assume which credential was sent, keep the fall-back to the card number, re-check each year the two fee lines that are moving (charges on stored-card transactions sent without a token, and charges for token and updater services), and ask who requested its tokens before counting on them in a change of provider.
thesis.how_why: EMVCo describes the token as constrained to a merchant, device or payment scenario, and because the network holds the mapping it can re-point the token when a card is reissued and attach a one-time cryptogram to a cardholder's use. The push is documented: Mastercard stated on 11 June 2024 a goal of 100% e-commerce tokenization in Europe by 2030, and processor bulletins report network fees since October 2023 on card-number transactions that are neither tokenized nor authenticated. The networks' stated reasons are less fraud and an end to manual card entry; that the push also moves control of the stored credential to the network is the chapter's reading of those facts and is labeled as the author's synthesis, not as a motive the networks have stated. The reported gains are the vendors' own: Visa's release of 4 June 2024 says a 'six-basis point' approval increase, Adyen (2024) reports 3% on average, and Stripe reports 3.8% for a bundle of three features. The two providers expose tokens differently, as documented in November 2026: Stripe provisions them automatically and chooses token or card number per payment, showing the merchant a read-only field and documenting no integration for a merchant's own tokens; Adyen offers an Adyen-managed mode and a merchant-managed mode, returns per-attempt data, and supports tokens only on payments it acquires. Whether tokens a provider requested move with a merchant that leaves is answered for Adyen only: its terms (13 June 2025) describe a Network Token Sharing Service for use with other payment providers, with the cryptogram still supplied by Adyen; no Stripe statement was found.

role.contribution: Shows the second relocation: the stored credential moves from the provider's vault to the card network, and what the merchant gains and can no longer assume.

transition_in.carries_over: The provider token of chapter 22: an identifier that means something only inside one provider's vault and that the issuer never sees.
transition_in.introduces: A token issued by the card network, which travels through the acquirer to the issuer in place of the card number and stays valid when the card behind it changes.

posts.title: Deciding in Milliseconds: Fraud and Risk Systems
posts.question: How does a provider decide, during an authorization, whether a payment is fraud?

know: The fraud types (stolen cards, card testing, account takeover, friendly fraud, merchant fraud) and how the evidence for each arrives.
Where risk scoring sits in the authorization path at Stripe and at Adyen, and the two decision points before and after the issuer answers.

What Stripe has published about Radar's models (2023 and 2026) and what Adyen has published about its fraud models (tree-based ensembles retrained weekly by default, 2024) and its bot-attack model (2026), and what neither has published.
What a merchant can configure: thresholds, rules, lists, reviews.
believe: A risk score is an estimate of a later dispute, and its threshold is a price the merchant sets between lost sales and fraud losses.
A change to a fraud model or rule cannot be judged on the first two weeks of results.
Card testing is a problem of traffic shape that has to be stopped before authorization.
can_do: Say what a given risk decision can and cannot know at the moment it is made.
Set or challenge a block threshold by comparing the cost of a refused good customer with the cost of a fraud case.
Recognize a card-testing attack from its symptoms and name the controls that stop it.
Explain why a fraud system needs a holdout of payments it lets through.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a merchant that judges a new fraud rule after two weeks, the reader names the two things the judgement cannot yet know.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A fashion retailer adds a rule that blocks every payment its provider scores as elevated risk. Two weeks later its fraud disputes are down and it declares the rule a success. What two things is that conclusion missing?
acceptance_criteria.expected: First, most fraud is not yet reported: cardholders take weeks to dispute (Stripe's 2026 figures: 41% of fraud disputes by day 14, 86% by day 60), so the before-and-after comparison is incomplete. Second, a blocked payment never gets a label, so the retailer has not measured how many good customers the rule refused; that needs a holdout or control group of payments let through.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a description of a card-testing attack on a merchant the chapter does not mention, the reader identifies it, says why a model trained on disputes does not catch it, and names where it must be stopped.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A charity's donation form suddenly receives thousands of €1 donations an hour from constantly changing IP addresses; most are declined by the card issuers. What is happening, why would a fraud model that learns from disputes be slow to see it, and where should it be stopped?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Card testing: criminals checking which stolen or guessed card numbers work. No single attempt carries a fraud label and most never become disputes, so the signal is in the shape of the traffic over minutes, not in any one payment. Declined attempts still cost fees and damage the merchant's standing with issuers and networks, so it must be stopped before the request reaches the issuer: rate limits, CAPTCHA or login in front of the form, and the provider's pre-authorization bot blocking.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every statement about Stripe's or Adyen's models carries its year, old sources are flagged with their age, and the chapter states what is not public: Adyen's fraud-risk model beyond its family and weekly retraining (2024), both companies' criteria and models for accepting a merchant, and Radar's current retraining interval (daily in a 2019 post).

thesis.question: How does a provider decide, during an authorization, whether a payment is fraud?
thesis.claim: A provider cannot know during an authorization whether a payment is fraud. It estimates, before the issuer sees the payment and inside the payment's time budget, how likely the payment is to be disputed as fraud later, using signals from many merchants, and blocks above a threshold; the facts it learns from arrive weeks afterwards and never arrive for payments it blocked, so each threshold trades refused legitimate customers against fraud losses, and the merchant bears both.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that fraud detection is the provider's job: its model classifies each payment as fraud or not, so a merchant who switches it on is protected and has nothing left to decide.
thesis.so_what: A merchant has to set the threshold from its own margins, judge any rule or model change only after the dispute labels have come in, use the provider's backtests and control group to see what its rules refuse, and put limits in front of any endpoint that can start a payment.
thesis.how_why: Both companies document a decision before the payment goes to the network (Stripe marks a blocked payment 'not_sent_to_network'; Adyen's pre-authorization rules) and a second after the issuer answers. The score predicts a dispute: Adyen's documentation says its risk level 'indicates the likelihood that a transaction will result in a fraudulent dispute'. Stripe's October 2026 engineering post gives the delay: 41% of fraud disputes are reported by day 14, 66% by day 30 and 86% by day 60, and a larger model that looked better at first was rolled back once later labels arrived. Because a blocked payment has no outcome, Adyen documents 'control traffic' and Stripe documents altering the score for a small subset of payments, which the chapter reads, as an inference, as a holdout. Card testing has no per-payment label at all, and its declined attempts still cost the merchant fees and standing with issuers, so it has to be stopped before authorization. A refused legitimate customer is a sale the merchant loses, and for accepted fraud Stripe states that the merchant is 'ultimately responsible for payments you choose to accept'. The public record is uneven: Stripe has described Radar's model lineage (to a neural-network-only model in mid-2022, per its 2023 post) and exposes a 0–99 score; Adyen has described its bot-attack feature pipeline (October 2026) and, for its fraud models, tree-based ensembles retrained weekly by default (August 2024), exposes five risk levels, and lets each rule run before or after authorization. Stripe's 'less than 100 milliseconds' is from 2023; Adyen gives 20 ms median and 100 ms at the 99th percentile per model endpoint (January 2025) and no figure for the whole risk decision.

role.contribution: Shows the third relocation: the allow-or-block decision moves to the provider's model while the loss stays with the merchant, and supplies the fraud rate and risk score that authentication exemptions depend on.

transition_in.carries_over: Chapters 22 and 23 protected the credential: the number is in a vault, or replaced by a token restricted to one merchant.
transition_in.introduces: The problem those controls leave open: a card number stolen elsewhere is typed into the checkout by someone who is not the cardholder, and something has to judge each use of a card, not the storage of it.

posts.title: Proving It Is You: 3-D Secure and Strong Customer Authentication
posts.question: How does the issuer check who is paying, and how do providers decide when to ask?

know: What strong customer authentication requires under PSD2, its exemptions with their thresholds, and why merchant-initiated payments fall outside it.
The parts and flows of EMV 3-D Secure 2: the 3DS server, directory server and access control server; frictionless and challenge.
When a successful authentication moves the fraud loss to the issuer and when it does not.
How Stripe and Adyen each expose authentication decisions, as documented in November 2026, and the status of PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation on 17 November 2026.
believe: Whether to authenticate is a decision about who carries a fraud loss, weighed against customers lost to a challenge.
The issuer, not the merchant or the provider, has the last word on whether the payer is challenged.
A provider's capacity to request exemptions depends on the fraud rate of all its merchants together.
can_do: For a given payment, say whether authentication is required, which exemption could apply, and who carries the loss under each outcome.
Design a membership or subscription so that the first payment is authenticated and later ones are correctly marked as merchant-initiated.
Model a payment that needs authentication as a state the client must resolve, not as one synchronous call.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a payment that skipped authentication under an exemption and turned out to be fraud, the reader says who bears the loss and what would have changed that.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A Dutch bookshop's provider skips the 3-D Secure check on a €40 online payment by requesting a low-risk exemption (the rule that lets a payment judged low-risk go without two-factor authentication). The issuer agrees. The payment later turns out to be fraud. Who bears the loss, and what would have had to happen for someone else to bear it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The bookshop: when the merchant's side requests the exemption and the issuer grants it, there is no liability shift. Had the payment been authenticated through 3-D Secure, or had the issuer applied the exemption on its own without being asked, the issuer would have carried the fraud dispute.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a recurring product the chapter does not use as its example, the reader says which payment must be authenticated and what the later ones are.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A language-learning app in Germany sells a €12 monthly plan paid by card. Which payment has to be authenticated by the cardholder, why do the later ones not, and who carries the loss if a later one is disputed as fraud?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The first payment, when the cardholder sets up the series, needs strong customer authentication. Later charges are initiated by the merchant with the payer absent, so they are outside the rule; like an exemption, they involve no challenge and no liability shift, so the app carries a fraud dispute on them.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter states that PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation were not adopted on 17 November 2026, attributes its description of their content to the secondary reading it comes from, and marks scheme passkeys as in pilot or first rollout.

thesis.question: How does the issuer check who is paying, and how do providers decide when to ask?
thesis.claim: The issuer checks the payer through 3-D Secure, either silently from transaction and device data the merchant's side sends or by challenging the cardholder, and the issuer has the final say on which; a provider decides when to ask by weighing the customers a challenge would lose against the fraud loss the merchant keeps whenever a payment goes through unauthenticated, within what the law requires, because the loss moves to the issuer only when authentication happens.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that authentication is friction and nothing else: an exemption or a skipped challenge saves a customer and changes nothing besides, so the right policy is always to authenticate as rarely as the rules allow.
thesis.so_what: A team should set its authentication policy as a loss-allocation policy: know for each kind of payment whether an exemption, a merchant-initiated flag or a full authentication applies and who pays for fraud in each case, and expect the limits to move with the provider's fraud rate and with regulation.
thesis.how_why: Stripe's documentation says it cannot guarantee a requested flow 'because the issuer determines the ultimate authentication flow'. PSD2 Article 74(2) puts the loss on the side that does not require or accept strong authentication, and the network rules follow: Adyen's documentation says that when the acquirer requests a low-risk exemption 'the chargeback liability stays with you', and Stripe's says that when the bank approves an exemption request 'liability shift for fraudulent transactions doesn't apply'. Merchant-initiated payments are out of scope and likewise carry no shift. The low-risk exemption is rationed by the provider's own fraud rate (0.13%, 0.06% and 0.01% for payments up to €100, €250 and €500 in the 2018 technical standards), so one merchant's ceiling depends on every other merchant at that provider. Both providers now make the choice by model and expose rules as constraints, with documented differences (November 2026): Stripe requests 3-D Secure through Radar rules and publishes its exemption ceiling of €250; Adyen keeps a separate ordered list of Dynamic 3-D Secure rules, returns the exemption it requested on each payment, and argued in September 2026 that being authentication provider and acquirer in one lets its models learn from authorization outcomes. Method selection beyond 3-D Secure (scheme passkeys) is documented at Adyen as a pilot, with a first rollout in the UK announced on 29 October 2026; for Stripe an undated support article describes Stripe Authentication, a device-verification method in trial, and its product page and a Sessions 2026 talk describe an engine that selects the authentication pathway, which its documentation does not. PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation were not adopted on 17 November 2026.

role.contribution: Shows the fourth relocation and the only one in the part that moves a loss outright: authentication shifts a fraud dispute to the issuer, and exemptions keep it where it was.

transition_in.carries_over: The risk rule of chapter 24 had a third action between allow and block, 'request 3-D Secure', and the merchant was left carrying the loss on every payment it allowed.
transition_in.introduces: What that third action is: handing the question of who is paying to the issuer, and the conditions under which the issuer then takes the fraud loss as well.

posts.title: Know Your Customer, Watch the Money: Compliance as a System
posts.question: What must a payment company know about its customers and their transactions, and how does that become software?

know: The duties in outline: verifying a business and its beneficial owners, sanctions and politically-exposed-person screening, transaction monitoring and suspicious-activity reporting, periodic re-verification.
How Stripe and Adyen each expose verification to a platform: requirements or verification errors, deadlines and capabilities, as documented in November 2026.

The regulatory dates that matter as of November 2026: DORA in application since 17 January 2025, the EU anti-money-laundering regulation from 10 July 2027, instant payments and verification of payee, and PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation not yet adopted.
What neither company publishes: transaction-monitoring scenarios, sanctions-screening logic, re-verification intervals.
believe: Onboarding is the first run of a loop: an account that was fully enabled can become restricted later without the seller doing anything.
A provider's verification does not discharge a platform's own obligations, and a missed deadline shows up as stopped payouts.
can_do: Design a platform's handling of verification as mirrored state: requirements, deadlines, capability status, an owner for each deadline, and a way to tell the seller.
Given a seller whose payouts stopped, list the causes the providers' documented models allow and where to look.
Tell apart fraud scoring and anti-money-laundering monitoring by timing and output.
Place a regulatory change on the calendar with its status: in application, adopted with a future date, or not adopted.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a seller whose payouts stop long after onboarding with no action on the seller's part, the reader names at least two causes consistent with the documented models and what the platform should have had in place.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A marketplace for second-hand furniture onboarded a seller a year ago, and payouts have worked ever since. This morning the seller's payouts stopped. The seller changed nothing. Name two explanations that fit how payment providers handle verification, and say what the marketplace should have had in place.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Two of: a requirement changed or a new one became due and its deadline passed; the seller crossed a volume or time threshold that needs more information; a periodic review asked the seller to confirm its data; a sanctions, ownership or other compliance review opened. The marketplace should store each seller's outstanding requirements, deadlines and capability status from the provider's API and webhooks, show them to the seller, and have a named owner and a monitored channel for every deadline.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a proposal to reuse the fraud engine for money-laundering monitoring, the reader states how the two differ in timing and output.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An engineer proposes to detect money laundering with the same component that scores payments for fraud during authorization (the real-time request to the cardholder's bank). Give two ways in which the two jobs differ.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Fraud scoring decides in milliseconds on one payment and its output is allow, block or challenge. Money-laundering monitoring looks at behavior over days or weeks after the fact, and its output is a case for a person, possibly a confidential report to an authority or a freeze, which the customer may not be told about. They can share data; they should not share a decision path.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter states that neither Stripe nor Adyen publishes how it monitors transactions or screens against sanctions lists, and labels its own account of those systems as reference-architecture inference.
The chapter's conclusion performs the part's closing: it connects the five controls to one another, returns to the Card-Testing Weekend beside the Frozen Studios, and hands off to billing.

thesis.question: What must a payment company know about its customers and their transactions, and how does that become software?
thesis.claim: A payment company must know who each business it serves and pays is, who owns and controls it, whether any of them is under sanctions, and whether its transactions look like money laundering, and it must keep knowing this for as long as it serves that business; in software the verification duties become state on an account, made of requirements with deadlines that switch capabilities such as payouts on and off, and that state can change months after onboarding without the customer doing anything. How the monitoring of transactions becomes software is not public for Stripe or Adyen.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that compliance is an onboarding form: identity is checked once at sign-up, the provider takes care of it, and an approved seller stays approved.
thesis.so_what: A platform that embeds payments must store and display each seller's verification state and give every deadline an owner, because the provider enforces a missed requirement by stopping the seller's payouts, and the provider's checks do not replace the platform's own legal duties.
thesis.how_why: The duties are continuous by law: sanctions lists change and must be re-checked on new designations, ownership changes, and the EU regulation that applies from 10 July 2027 caps the interval between reviews at one year for higher-risk customers and five years for others. A one-time record cannot satisfy that, so both providers model verification as account state that gates capabilities and deliver changes by webhook. Stripe's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) lists requirements as currently due, eventually due and past due against a deadline, announces rule changes in a 'future_requirements' structure, and warns: 'Don't rely on Stripe's verification to meet any independent legal KYC or verification requirements.' Adyen's documents capabilities with a verification status, standard deadlines of 30 or 60 days, and a periodic data review as an API flow; Stripe's own periodic re-verification is announced (support article, last updated October 2026) and in preview, and Adyen announces rule changes in release notes without an API structure. That difference, Stripe exposing rule changes in its API and Adyen the periodic review, is what the public record shows. How either company monitors transactions or screens against sanctions lists, and at what intervals it re-verifies, is not public, and part of it may not lawfully be disclosed to the customer concerned; the chapter describes those systems only as labeled inference.

role.contribution: Shows the fifth relocation, from the payer's side to the seller's: the duty to know the customer sits with the provider and returns to the platform as state to track; the chapter also carries the part's closing.

transition_in.carries_over: Four chapters about the payer and the card: where the number is kept, which credential is sent, whether the payment looks like fraud, whether the cardholder was authenticated. Each was a decision about one payment.
transition_in.introduces: The other end of the payment: the business being paid, which the provider must know and keep knowing, as a standing state on an account instead of a decision per payment.

parts.title: Part VI — REVENUE: Billing, Tax and Recognition

know: What a billing engine adds to a payment API: a scheduler, a price calculator and a subscription state machine whose output is an invoice.

The terms the part owns: subscription, billing cycle, proration, usage event, meter, rating, invoice, credit note, dunning, involuntary churn, tax registration, deemed supplier, deferred revenue, performance obligation, merchant of record.

What Stripe documents for billing, metering, invoicing, recovery, tax, revenue recognition and merchant of record as of November 2026, what Adyen documents (token payments with recurring flags, Auto Rescue, account updating, the Orb acquisition closed on 1 July 2026), where no public source on Adyen was found, and where Adyen has stated its position (it does not act as a merchant of record).
believe: Recurring revenue is a second state machine driven by the clock, and its failures are failures of time: a charge that is late, taken twice, or counted in the wrong period.
The invoice, not the payment, is the unit of revenue: it is what gets scheduled, filled with usage, collected, taxed and recognized.
A provider's tax, recognition or merchant-of-record product covers the transactions and contracts that provider sees, and the obligation it does not explicitly take over stays with the seller.
can_do: Given a billing incident, say whether it was late, twice or in the wrong period, and name the period, key or cut-off that should have prevented it.

For a recurring or usage-priced product, list the decisions a team must make before the first invoice: period boundaries and time zone, proration rule, event acceptance and correction rules, retry policy per decline type and payment method, tax registrations, and the data finance needs per invoice line.
For a stated business on Stripe, on Adyen or on both, say which of these jobs the provider's documented products do and which must live in the business's own system or a third-party one.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.
A reader who has read only Part VI classifies three billing faults in a case the part does not contain as late, twice and wrong period, and names the mechanism for each.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A meal-kit company bills a weekly box. After a deploy, some customers were charged twice for the same week; others were charged three days late and first received a 'your payment failed' email; and finance's March revenue includes, in full, one-year gift subscriptions paid in March. Using Part VI: what kind of failure is each, and what should have prevented it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Twice: the charge was not tied to one invoice per subscription and period, so a second run created a second charge; a key or invoice per period prevents it. Late: the scheduler, not the customer, was late, and dunning was started by a missing payment instead of by a failed attempt on a finalized invoice. Wrong period: cash was reported as revenue; the annual amount is deferred revenue released over the service period.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader can say, for each job in the part, whether Adyen's public documentation covers it as of November 2026, without presenting an absence of documentation as a statement by Adyen, or a statement by Adyen as an absence.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A team that processes payments on Adyen needs: a subscription schedule with proration, retries of failed renewals, VAT calculation on its invoices, a revenue schedule for annual plans, and a provider that acts as the merchant of record. According to Part VI, which of these does Adyen's public documentation describe as of November 2026, and what does the part say about the rest?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Described: retrying failed merchant-initiated payments (Auto Rescue) and updating stored card details, both at the level of the payment. Stated by Adyen: it does not act as a merchant of record (its article of 15 September 2026). Not found in public sources: a first-party subscription or invoice object, tax engine or revenue-recognition product; Adyen's terms leave each party its own tax obligations. Orb was acquired on 1 July 2026 and has billing and recognition features of its own, and Orb's documentation describes Adyen as a payment gateway for Orb invoices, but no billing product is documented as part of Adyen's platform. The part states the absences as gaps in the public record, to be filled by the merchant's own or a third-party system, not as confirmed facts about Adyen.

thesis.question: What has to be built on top of a payment API before single payments become recurring, usage-priced, taxed and reportable revenue, and how does that system fail?
thesis.claim: Revenue needs a second state machine on top of payments, driven by the clock and by billing periods instead of by a customer's click: it decides what is owed, for which period and when to ask, and hands the payment engine an invoice. Its failures are failures of time (a charge that is late, taken twice, or counted in the wrong period), and whoever holds the invoice is the only party that can collect it as a debt, tax it and recognize it. As of November 2026 the public record puts that machine inside Stripe's platform and outside Adyen's.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that billing is a thin layer of configuration over payments (a monthly job that charges saved cards, plus reports for finance), so that a provider with good authorization rates and stored credentials has already solved the hard part.
thesis.so_what: A team that accepts the claim designs renewals around the invoice and its period, not around the charge; asks of any provider 'where does the invoice live?' before comparing features; and, where the provider holds no invoice, budgets for a billing system of its own or a third party's.
thesis.how_why: A customer-started payment has one moment and one amount. A recurring charge has neither until something computes them: a scheduler picks the instant, a price plan and a usage count give the amount, and a state machine says what the subscription is while the invoice is unpaid. Each of those depends on time boundaries (period start, event cut-off, retry window, tax point, service period), and each boundary is a place where a charge can land late, twice or in the wrong period. Stripe documents subscription, invoice, meter, tax and revenue-recognition objects on one platform. Adyen documents stored tokens charged with a recurring flag, payment-level retry and card updating, and closed its acquisition of the billing company Orb on 1 July 2026; no integrated Adyen billing product, tax engine or revenue-recognition product was found in public sources, and Adyen states that it does not act as a merchant of record, so several comparisons in this part are between Stripe's product and what a merchant must supply itself.

supporting_claims.claim: A billing engine is a scheduler, a price calculator and a subscription state machine whose output is an invoice; the payment API executes only its last step.

Usage can be billed correctly only if three time rules are fixed before the first invoice (how long an event is accepted, when the period's invoice closes, how a wrong event is corrected), because usage events arrive late and twice.

Between owed and paid, what is recovered is the debt on a finalized invoice, through as many attempts and payment methods as it takes; a provider that holds the invoice retries a debt, and one that sees only payments retries a payment.

Tax and revenue recognition are second readings of the same invoice lines, by place and by period, and a provider can compute them only for the sales and contracts it sees; the liability and the accounting judgement stay with the seller.

As of November 2026 the public record shows the billing state machine inside Stripe's platform and outside Adyen's: Adyen documents recurring token payments, payment-level retry and an Orb acquisition closed on 1 July 2026 with no documented integrated product, so for invoicing, tax, recognition and merchant of record the comparison is Stripe's product against the merchant's own or a third-party system.

Making the provider the merchant of record puts its name on the customer's statement and invoice and hands it the indirect tax and the handling of fraud and disputes; under the one arrangement documented in detail as of November 2026, Stripe's, the cost of disputes, refunds and reversals, the seller-of-record role and the revenue stay with the business. The price is a fee, the checkout, the statement name and part of the customer relationship; it is an operating model, and it does not fit a platform that pays other sellers.

role.contribution: Shows that the gap between instant answer and slow truth repeats one level up: a renewal 'succeeds' or 'fails' on a schedule nobody watches, and the truth about what was owed, taxed and earned arrives later still. Without this part the book would explain single payments and leave out the system that starts most of them.

additional_patterns.applies_to: subscriptions-and-billing-engines to invoicing-collections-and-dunning: one billing period in the order it happens, from the scheduler through the usage count to the invoice and its collection
billing-and-payment-tax and billing-revenue-recognition: the two calculations that read a finalized invoice

flow.rationale: The invoice is built up chapter by chapter. Chapter 27 defines the subscription, the period and the invoice as the engine's output; chapter 28 needs the period to say when usage stops counting toward it; chapter 29 needs both to explain finalization and what is being collected; tax (30) and recognition (31) read the finalized invoice's lines, credit notes and refunds, which chapter 29 owns; and merchant of record (32) can be judged only after the reader has seen every obligation it takes over. Putting tax or recognition before invoicing would ask the reader to tax and schedule a document whose immutability and corrections have not been explained; putting merchant of record first would present it as a shortcut before the reader knows what it is a shortcut around. Three of the six transitions are not sequence because the chapters do different work: 28 breaks the fixed-amount assumption of 27, and 32 answers the burden that 27 to 31 accumulate.

hook.content: On 1 October 2026 Larkfield's renewal job hit its provider's rate limit and 7,900 membership renewals slipped to the next day; dunning emails went to members who had done nothing wrong. On 1 November 2026 a provider call timed out, the same job retried with a new idempotency key, and 1,840 members were charged twice; €71,300 was refunded and 212 members disputed the charge anyway. Every card payment that ran in those two months did what it was asked. The fault was in the thing that decides when to ask, and for which month.

opening.bridge: From Parts I to V, where a customer starts each payment and the question is whether it was approved, recorded and safe, to payments that nobody present starts: a clock does, for a period, from a stored credential. The reader's own experience of this is a subscription that renewed without them noticing, or failed without them knowing why.
opening.roadmap: Six chapters in the order of one billing period and what follows from it: the billing engine and its subscription state machine; counting usage before charging for it; the invoice, its collection and what happens when the first attempt fails; tax on the invoice; revenue recognition and the hand-off to finance; and the model in which the provider sells in its own name as the merchant of record. The part says up front that Adyen's side of the tax, recognition and merchant-of-record chapters is short: no first-party Adyen tax or recognition product was found in public sources, and Adyen states that it does not act as a merchant of record.

closing.synthesis: Every chapter of the part turned out to be about one document. The scheduler exists to produce the invoice, metering fills it, dunning collects it, tax and recognition read it, and merchant of record changes whose name is on it. So the question that sorts billing architectures, and the two providers, is not which features each has but where the invoice lives: the party that holds it knows what is owed, for which period, by whom and to whom, and every other party sees only payments with a reference.
closing.so_what: A reader evaluating a provider, or a build-versus-buy decision for billing, can ask one question first (who holds the invoice and its period?) and predict from the answer who will do the retries, the tax, the revenue schedule and the corrections.
closing.callback: Larkfield's 1 October and 1 November 2026: late, then twice. Keel's answers to both are billing-engine decisions taken inside a payments program: K1 derives the idempotency key for a renewal from the membership id, the billing period and the number of the scheduled attempt, and K5 has the renewal job pace itself over 18 hours and retry on a schedule tied to decline codes.

takeaway.content: For every recurring charge in your own system, write down the period it is for, derive its key from that period, and name the one system that holds the invoice. Then check each of the part's jobs (retry, tax, recognition, correction) against that system, not against the payment provider's feature list.

transition_in.carries_over: From Part V and the parts before it: stored credentials and network tokens, merchant-initiated payments that run without the cardholder present, the payment state machine and idempotency keys, and Part V's point that a control moves liability between parties without removing it.
transition_in.introduces: Payments that no customer starts. A clock starts them, for a billing period, which adds a second state machine above the payment and a new kind of failure: not declined or fraudulent, but late, twice or in the wrong period. The question of who carries a liability returns at the end of the part as the merchant of record.

posts.title: Part VI — REVENUE: Billing, Tax and Recognition
posts.question: What does Part VI argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?

know: Part VI argues that revenue needs a second, time-driven state machine above payments, whose output is the invoice and whose failures are late, twice and wrong period.
The six chapters follow one billing period: engine, usage, invoice and collection, tax, recognition, merchant of record.

The Adyen side of several chapters is short: no first-party Adyen tax, invoicing or revenue-recognition product was found in public sources as of November 2026, and Adyen states that it does not act as a merchant of record.
can_do: Pick the chapter of Part VI that answers the billing question in front of them.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can state the part's claim and name the six chapters' subjects in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what does Part VI argue, and what will each of the next six chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Billing is a second state machine driven by time, and it fails by being late, twice or in the wrong period. Then: the billing engine and subscriptions; usage metering and rating; invoicing, collections and dunning; tax; revenue recognition; merchant of record.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page opens with the two dated Larkfield renewal incidents themselves (1 October and 1 November 2026, with their figures), not with a description of billing.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: the two renewal incidents, the part thesis, the reading order, and the warning that the public record on Adyen is thin for half the part.

posts.title: Charging Again and Again: Subscriptions and the Billing Engine
posts.question: What does a billing engine do that a payment API does not?

know: The parts of a billing engine (scheduler, price calculator, subscription state machine) and the objects Stripe documents for them: product, price, subscription, schedule, invoice, and the payment created for an invoice.
What a billing cycle anchor, a proration and a subscription status are, and how Stripe documents month ends, UTC instants, eight statuses and two billing modes.

That Adyen's documented recurring model is a stored token charged with a declared processing model, and that Orb, acquired on 1 July 2026, is not documented as part of Adyen's platform as of November 2026.
believe: A subscription is a state machine that produces invoices, not a job that charges a card.
Billing rules such as proration are part of the agreement with the customer and cannot be changed under invoices already issued.
can_do: List the decisions their own code must make if they run renewals on a bare payment API.
Say, for a given provider, where the schedule, the amount and the invoice live.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a subscription case the chapter does not contain, the reader names the decisions a billing engine makes that a payment API does not.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A language-learning app charges €12 a month. A customer signs up on 31 January and, halfway through March, moves to the €20 plan. The team uses only a payment API with saved cards. Which decisions does their own code now have to make?
acceptance_criteria.expected: On which day the February charge falls (the last day of the month) and at which instant and in which time zone a period starts; what the unused half of the old price is worth and what the rest of the new one costs (proration), and whether that is charged now or on the next invoice; what identifies each period's charge so a retry does not charge it twice; and what state the subscription is in while a charge is unpaid.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can state what Adyen's documentation provides for recurring payments and what must be supplied elsewhere, with the Orb acquisition's status as of November 2026.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A colleague says 'we are on Adyen, so Adyen handles our subscriptions'. From this chapter: what does Adyen's documentation provide, and what has to live somewhere else?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Adyen provides a stored token and a merchant-initiated payment flagged as a subscription payment. The schedule, the amount, proration, the invoice and the subscription's state live in the merchant's system or a billing system connected to Adyen. Adyen bought the billing company Orb (closed 1 July 2026), which still runs as a stand-alone product; no integrated Adyen billing product is documented as of November 2026.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every statement about how Stripe's scheduler or Adyen's platform works internally is either a dated documented fact or a labeled inference, and the chapter says where the public record on renewal scheduling stops: one 2024 Stripe engineering post describes a scheduling service, and neither company has published how that work is partitioned, paced or kept from running twice.

thesis.question: What does a billing engine do that a payment API does not?
thesis.claim: A billing engine decides what is owed, for which period and when to ask: it is a scheduler, a price calculator and a subscription state machine whose output is an invoice, and the payment API executes only the last step. Stripe keeps that engine in its platform, with subscription, invoice and payment as separate objects; Adyen's documentation offers a stored token charged with a recurring flag and leaves the schedule, the amount and the invoice to the merchant or a connected billing system, and Orb, acquired on 1 July 2026, is not documented as part of Adyen's platform as of November 2026.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a subscription is a monthly job that charges a saved card, so a payment API with stored credentials is enough and a billing engine is packaging around it.
thesis.so_what: A team choosing between running renewals itself and using a billing engine knows what it is taking on: period boundaries, a proration rule it cannot change later, a status for every unpaid state, and one charge per period. A team on Adyen knows it must name the system that holds those, because the payment provider does not.
thesis.how_why: Charging on a clock raises questions a customer-started payment never asks: what 'the 31st' means in February, at which instant a period starts (Stripe stores anchors as UTC seconds), what a mid-period plan change is worth, and what a subscription is while its invoice is unpaid. Stripe's documentation answers each with a rule: eight subscription statuses, month-end anchoring, proration to the second, and since 2025 two billing modes with one-way migration, which the chapter reads, as a labeled inference, as a sign that billing rules cannot be changed in place once invoices exist. The public record stops at the scheduler itself: Stripe documents its visible timing (a renewal invoice stays in draft for about an hour, and finalization waits for webhook acknowledgment) and one 2024 Stripe engineering post describes a scheduling service that finds subscriptions whose billing periods have just ended and triggers a new invoice; no Stripe or Adyen publication describes how that work is partitioned, paced or kept from running twice.

role.contribution: Defines the second state machine and its output, the invoice, which every later chapter of the part fills, collects or reads; and establishes where that machine sits on each provider.

transition_in.carries_over: The part intro's claim that something above the payment decides when to ask and for which month, shown by Larkfield's late and doubled renewals.
transition_in.introduces: What that something is made of: a scheduler, a price calculator and a subscription state machine, with the invoice as the object it hands to the payment engine.

posts.title: Counting Before Charging: Usage Metering and Rating
posts.question: How do you bill for usage when events arrive late, twice and by the billion?

know: What a usage event, a meter, rating, a credit balance and a commitment are.

The limits Stripe documents for its meters (events accepted up to 35 days back, a finalization grace period of 1 hour by default and up to 72 hours, cancellation within 24 hours) and the design Stripe described in January 2025 (stream aggregation with a 30-second path and a five-minute durable path).

That Orb's documentation describes the other design (immutable raw events, invoices computed by query), and that Stripe completed its acquisition of Metronome on 14 January 2026 and Adyen its acquisition of Orb on 1 July 2026.
believe: An event that is accepted is not thereby an event that is billed; the two are separate rules.
A duplicate can be removed only by an identifier the producer of the event assigned.
can_do: Write a late-event policy for a usage-priced product: acceptance window, billing cut-off and correction path.
Say whether a requirement needs a real-time balance or invoice-time rating, and what each costs.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given duplicated and late usage in a case the chapter does not contain, the reader says what had to be decided beforehand for each.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An API company bills per request. Its gateway resends a batch after a timeout, so some requests are reported twice. A regional outage then delivers another batch three days after the month ended. For each problem: what must have been decided before the first invoice, and by whom?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Duplicates: each event carries an identifier assigned by the gateway that produced it, so the second report is dropped; an identifier generated on receipt removes nothing. Late batch: whether it is still inside the acceptance window, whether the month's invoice has already closed, and, if it has, which correction path applies (a later invoice, a credit note or an adjustment). The reader distinguishes accepted from billed.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can tell a real-time balance check from invoice-time rating and say which one a prepaid-credit requirement needs.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A customer has bought €50 of prepaid usage credit. Can the customer use €80 worth before anything stops them? What decides the answer?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Yes, if credit is applied only when the invoice is computed; no, if a balance is drawn down as usage is rated. These are two consistency requirements with different cost, and the chapter gives the documented example of each.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Statements about Orb's architecture are presented as Orb's documentation about Orb, not as facts about Adyen's platform, and no claim is made about Metronome's internal design.

thesis.question: How do you bill for usage when events arrive late, twice and by the billion?
thesis.claim: A usage invoice can stop changing and still be explained only if three time rules are fixed before the first invoice (how long an event is accepted, when the period's invoice closes, how a wrong event is corrected) and duplicates are removed by an identifier the producer assigns; volume then forces one design choice, to aggregate events as they arrive or to keep them raw and compute the invoice by query (raw where prices may change retroactively or an invoice must be explained from its events, aggregated where volume leaves no alternative), and the public record shows one documented example of each: Stripe's 2025 account of windowed stream aggregation and Orb's documentation of invoices computed from immutable events.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that metering is a counter (add one per event, multiply by the price at month end) and that the engineering problem is throughput, to be solved with a faster stream processor.
thesis.so_what: The reader sets the three rules on purpose instead of inheriting a vendor's defaults, knows that a provider can accept an event and still never bill it, and keeps raw events wherever a price may be changed retroactively or an invoice may have to be explained to an auditor.
thesis.how_why: An invoice has to stop changing while events keep arriving, so every usage system draws a line in time and needs a path for what lands after it. Stripe's meters accept events up to 35 days old, bill them only until the invoice is finalized plus a grace period (1 hour by default, at most 72), and allow cancellation for 24 hours; Orb documents a 12-hour grace period and amendments that archive events instead of overwriting them. Aggregating on arrival is cheap to query and loses the original events' context; computing from raw events keeps it and costs more per invoice. Both providers bought their usage engines in 2026 (Stripe completed Metronome on 14 January, Adyen completed Orb on 1 July). Stripe documents Metronome as pushing finished invoices into Stripe one way; Orb's design is documented by Orb about Orb; and the sources used say nothing of Metronome's internals, so the chapter does not place it on either side of the design choice.

role.contribution: Shows the time problem in its sharpest form: the amount owed for a period is unknown until a cut-off the system itself must choose, which is where 'late' and 'twice' enter billing before any payment is attempted.

transition_in.carries_over: The billing period, the invoice as the engine's output, and a price that is known the moment the period starts.
transition_in.introduces: A price that is not known until the period ends, because it depends on events that arrive late and more than once; counting them is a problem of its own before any invoice can be written.

posts.title: From Invoice to Cash: Invoicing, Collections and Dunning
posts.question: What happens between 'an amount is owed' and 'it has been paid', especially when the first attempt fails?

know: The invoice's states as Stripe documents them (draft, open, paid, void, uncollectible), what finalization fixes, and why corrections are credit notes.
What dunning and involuntary churn are; the difference between a hard and a soft decline for retry purposes; why direct debit needs its own retry rules.

What each provider documents for recovery: Stripe's Smart Retries on invoices (for new accounts, up to 8 retries within 2 weeks by default) and automatic card updates; Adyen's Auto Rescue on payments (a rescue window of one calendar month by default for cards) and its account updater, with Adyen's documentation pages cited as undated.
believe: What is being recovered is a debt on an invoice, not a failed payment.
Published recovery and churn percentages are vendor claims, nearly all without a stated baseline (Adyen's 2020 retry experiment is the exception), and the chapter's argument does not depend on them.
can_do: Design a dunning policy that branches on decline type and payment method and ends in a defined subscription state.
Correct a finalized invoice without editing it.
On a provider that holds no invoice, say how retry results are tied back to the invoice in their own system.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two failed renewals with different causes in a case the chapter does not contain, the reader prescribes different handling and gives the reason.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A streaming service has two failed renewals of €9.99. The first card payment came back 'stolen card'. The second, a SEPA Direct Debit (a bank debit the customer authorized in advance), came back days later as 'insufficient funds'. What should the collection process do in each case, and why not the same thing?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Stolen card is a hard decline: retrying that card cannot succeed, so the process asks the customer for a new payment method and retries only once one exists. Insufficient funds on a direct debit can be retried, but the failure arrives days late and the number of retries is capped, so it needs its own, slower schedule. In both cases the debt is the same invoice.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader corrects a finalized invoice by a credit note or by voiding and reissuing, and can say why editing is not allowed.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An invoice for €500 was finalized yesterday with the wrong customer address and €50 too much. What do you do, and why can you not just fix the invoice?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Issue a credit note for the €50, or void the invoice and issue a corrected copy for the address; a finalized invoice is kept as it was issued because tax rules commonly require it to be retained unchanged.

acceptance_criteria.statement: No involuntary-churn share or recovery rate appears without attribution to the vendor that published it, and the chapter states that no independent measurement was found.

thesis.question: What happens between 'an amount is owed' and 'it has been paid', especially when the first attempt fails?
thesis.claim: Between owed and paid stands the invoice: once finalized it is frozen, and it is then collected as one debt through as many attempts, payment methods and partial payments as it takes, so recovery acts on the debt and not on the failed payment. Which party holds the invoice decides what a provider can recover: Stripe retries an invoice it holds (Smart Retries, by default up to 8 retries within 2 weeks on new accounts), while Adyen's Auto Rescue retries a payment linked to the billing cycle only by a reference the merchant supplies, and the invoice stays in the merchant's system.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a failed renewal is a payment problem solved by charging the card again on a fixed schedule, and that the invoice is a PDF produced afterwards for the customer's records.
thesis.so_what: The reader models retries against the invoice, so that a new card, a bank transfer or a partial payment can all settle the same debt; separates hard from soft declines before scheduling anything; gives direct debit its own schedule; and, on Adyen, plans to hold the invoice state and join Auto Rescue results to it by reference.
thesis.how_why: Finalization assigns the number and freezes the fields that matter for tax, which Stripe's documentation explains by the requirement to retain invoices as issued; every later change is a credit note. Because the debt outlives any one attempt, the useful questions are whether another attempt can succeed at all (Stripe schedules but does not execute retries on hard declines until a new payment method appears; SEPA and Bacs debits get at most 2 retries in 30 days) and whether the credential can be repaired first (Stripe's network-dependent automatic card updates; Adyen's Real Time Account Updater, which checks for new card details and retries inside the same refused payment). The public record on the retry logic is one engineering post each: Stripe's of 23 January 2024 on Smart Retries ('more than 500 attributes') and Adyen's of 3 December 2020 on Auto Rescue (a contextual bandit; 'about 6% more orders than the baseline' in one experiment); neither publishes the model now running or the timing for a given decline. Stripe's recovery figures and the one customer result Adyen has published for Auto Rescue are vendor claims without definitions, and no independent measurement of involuntary churn was found, so the chapter quotes no churn share.

role.contribution: Supplies the invoice's state machine and the collection process, the place where the part's 'late' failure is handled on purpose, and the clearest documented consequence of where the billing engine sits on each provider.

transition_in.carries_over: An amount owed for a period, whether fixed by the plan (chapter 27) or counted from usage (chapter 28), and the cut-off after which it stops changing.
transition_in.introduces: The step from owed to paid: the invoice as a frozen document, the attempts made against it, and the process that runs when the first attempt fails.

posts.title: Whose Tax, at What Rate: Tax Calculation in the Payment Path
posts.question: How does indirect tax get calculated, collected and reported when the payment provider is also the tax engine?

know: At an introductory level, what VAT, GST and sales tax are, what a tax registration and a threshold are, and what a deemed supplier is.
The four steps Stripe's documentation names (know where you must collect, register, calculate and collect, file and remit) and which of them Stripe Tax performs as of November 2026.
That no public source was found describing an Adyen product that calculates, collects or files tax on a merchant's sales, and that this is an absence of evidence.
believe: A provider's tax product is a calculator with partial sight: the registrations, the sales it does not see and the liability remain the seller's.
For a platform, who owes the tax is a property of each transaction that the payment flow has to carry.
can_do: Say which facts and which state a tax calculation needs and where in a checkout or billing flow they are available.
Spot when a provider's threshold monitoring undercounts, and name the two ways to fix it.
Ask whether a platform is a deemed supplier for its category before designing its funds flow.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a business that sells through more than one channel, the reader explains why one provider's threshold monitoring can be wrong and what to do.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A software company takes 60% of its sales through a provider that has a tax feature and 40% through another provider. The tax feature's monitor says no new tax registration is needed anywhere. Why might that be wrong, and what are the two ways to fix it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The monitor counts only the sales that provider processed, while a registration threshold applies to all of the seller's sales into a territory. Fix: import the other sales into the tax product, or use a tax engine that is independent of both providers. Either way, confirming the obligation remains the seller's job.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can explain why a calculated tax of zero is not proof that no tax is due.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A provider's tax calculation returns €0 tax on a sale to a consumer in another country. Give one reason, from this chapter, why that may not mean 'no tax is due'.
acceptance_criteria.expected: The calculation returns zero wherever the seller has not recorded a registration, so zero can mean 'not registered here', which may itself be the problem if a threshold has been passed. An accepted alternative: a customer tax number that made the sale look business-to-business was not validated.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The Adyen column of the comparison says 'nothing public found' where that is the case, names where the search was made, and does not infer an Adyen design from the absence.

thesis.question: How does indirect tax get calculated, collected and reported when the payment provider is also the tax engine?
thesis.claim: A provider can calculate indirect tax because the checkout or invoice it runs already holds the three facts the calculation needs (who sells, what is sold, where the customer is), but calculating and collecting is one of four steps (know where tax is due, register, calculate and collect, file and remit) and the liability stays with the seller: Stripe Tax returns zero where the seller has recorded no registration, monitors thresholds only on the sales it sees, and as of November 2026 files itself only in the United States and for selected registrations in Ireland and Canada. The comparison is one-sided: no public source shows an Adyen product that calculates, collects or files tax on a merchant's sales, so on Adyen tax is computed by the merchant's own system or a separate tax engine.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that switching on a provider's tax feature makes tax the provider's responsibility; and the opposite view that tax belongs wholly to finance and the ERP and has no place in the payment path.
thesis.so_what: The reader treats a provider's tax product as a calculator fed by the provider's own data: registrations are state the business must maintain, a business on two providers (as Larkfield is) must feed the other provider's sales in or use an independent engine, and a platform must record the liable party on each transaction.
thesis.how_why: The tax amount has to be on the invoice before it is finalized and correct at the moment of the charge, which is why calculation sits beside billing and checkout and not in the ledger. Whether tax is due at all depends on registration, and registration depends on thresholds counted across every channel: an EU-wide €10,000 threshold for cross-border consumer sales since 1 July 2021, and sales-based 'economic nexus' in US states since the Wayfair decision of 21 June 2018. For platforms the law can move the liability itself: the EU has treated marketplaces as deemed suppliers of certain goods since 2021, and the 2025 VAT in the Digital Age package extends the idea to short-term accommodation and road passenger transport from 1 July 2028. The public record stops early on the Adyen side: searches of Adyen's documentation, help center and product pages found no product that calculates, collects or files tax on a merchant's sales, which is absence of evidence and not a statement by Adyen. They found how Adyen taxes its own fees, a tax amount the merchant may send with a payment, a `VAT` split type that books an amount the platform supplies, the filing of US form 1099-K for platform sellers, and a clause in Adyen's terms under which each party complies with its own tax obligations; Orb's documentation says it connects to third-party tax providers. The chapter is short for that reason.

role.contribution: Adds the first of the two calculations that read the invoice, and the part's first chapter in which the comparison is Stripe's product against what a merchant must bring itself.

transition_in.carries_over: Chapter 29's statement that a finalized invoice is frozen for tax reasons, and that it carries the customer's address and tax number.
transition_in.introduces: The tax line on that invoice: who owes it, what decides the rate, and how much of the work a payment provider's tax product does.

posts.title: Cash Is Not Revenue: Revenue Recognition and the Hand-off to Finance
posts.question: How does a billing system turn invoices and payments into recognized revenue, and where should it stop?

know: Why cash, billings and revenue are three different numbers, and what a performance obligation, a revenue schedule and deferred revenue are, at an architect's level.
The five steps of IFRS 15 and ASC 606 (issued together in May 2014) in one line each.

How Stripe Revenue Recognition is documented: built on a double-entry ledger, each invoice line treated as one performance obligation and amortized evenly over its period, with rules and imports for the rest. No Adyen revenue-recognition product was found; Orb documents one of its own.
believe: A payments report is not a revenue report.
Recognition inside a billing provider fits a business whose contracts equal its invoices; past that point the schedule belongs in a finance system.
can_do: Say how much of an up-front payment is revenue on a given date and what the rest is.
Specify the export a billing engine owes finance: per invoice line, the amount net of tax, the service period and every later adjustment with its own date.
Recognize a contract that the provider's default method will get wrong.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given an up-front payment in a case the chapter does not contain, the reader splits it into recognized and deferred revenue and names the data needed to do so.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A customer pays €1,200 on 1 January for one year of a software service. On 31 March: how much of it is revenue, what is the rest called, and what must the billing system have recorded for finance to work this out?
acceptance_criteria.expected: About €300 is revenue (three of twelve months); about €900 is deferred revenue, a liability until the service is delivered. Needed: the invoice line's amount net of tax, the start and end of its service period, and any refund, dispute or credit note with its own date.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader identifies a contract for which invoice-line-equals-obligation recognition gives the wrong schedule.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A sales team sells, on one invoice line, a year of software access together with a one-day onboarding workshop held in the first week. Why might a billing provider's default revenue schedule be wrong for this sale, and what are the options?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The default treats the invoice line as a single obligation spread evenly over the year, but the workshop is a separate promise delivered at one point in time. Options: split the line, apply a rule or import that splits the treatment, or keep the schedule in a finance system fed by the billing data.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter links to RECONCILED for posting to the general ledger and does not re-teach it; it stops at the data the billing side must hand over.

thesis.question: How does a billing system turn invoices and payments into recognized revenue, and where should it stop?
thesis.claim: A billing system turns invoices into revenue by giving each invoice line a service period, deferring its amount and releasing it as the service is delivered, with every refund, dispute and credit note as a dated adjustment; it should stop where contracts stop matching invoices. Stripe Revenue Recognition is documented on exactly that assumption (each invoice line is one performance obligation, amortized evenly over its period), so it serves a business whose contracts equal its invoices, and beyond that the schedule belongs in a finance system that the billing engine feeds. Adyen documents no revenue-recognition product; its reports describe payments, settlement and fees.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that revenue is what was charged in the month, so the payment provider's report is the revenue report; and the opposite view that recognition is the ERP's business alone and the billing engine owes finance nothing but totals.
thesis.so_what: An architect can specify what the billing side must export whatever tool does the recognition: per invoice line, the amount net of tax, the service period, and each later adjustment with its own date; and, for usage, the date of the usage as well as the date of the invoice, because they fall in different accounting periods at every month end.
thesis.how_why: IFRS 15 and ASC 606 recognize revenue when a promise to the customer is fulfilled, which for a service is over time; the cash for an annual plan arrives on one day and is a liability until earned. That is the part's third time failure, the wrong period, and it is produced by reading a payments report as revenue. Stripe documents its product as a double-entry ledger over the activity inside Stripe, with one rule per transaction and CSV imports for what Stripe did not process, and reports that update hours later; Stripe's own product page calls it 'a centralised revenue subledger', and its output still has to reach the general ledger.
