Orb documents recognition from invoices and raw usage for its own product, which describes Orb and not Adyen's platform; no Adyen revenue-recognition product was found in its documentation, help center or site, where revenue recognition is mentioned only on an Orb partner page and in an article of 22 October 2026.

role.contribution: Supplies the part's third failure of time, the wrong period, and draws the line between what a billing engine must hand to finance and what finance must do itself.

transition_in.carries_over: Tax as a calculation that reads the invoice's lines and asks where the sale took place and who owes the tax.
transition_in.introduces: A second calculation that reads the same lines and asks a different question: in which period the amount counts as revenue. As with tax, the provider can compute it only for what it sees.

posts.title: Who Is the Seller? Merchant of Record as an Operating Model
posts.question: What changes when the provider, not you, is the merchant of record?

know: The difference between a processor, a payment facilitator and a merchant of record: who is the seller to the buyer, whose name is on the card statement, who owes the indirect tax, who handles a dispute and who pays for it.

What Stripe documents for Managed Payments as of November 2026: first in the preview API version 2026-02-25.preview and in a release version since 22 April 2026, 3.5% per successful transaction on top of payment fees, digital products sold directly, the customer sees 'Sold through Link', no Connect platforms, countries where the tax liability does not transfer, and service terms under which the business remains the seller of record and pays for disputes, refunds and reversals.
That Paddle and the app stores are the contrast cases, and that Adyen states it does not act as a merchant of record.
believe: Merchant of record is an operating model that changes the checkout, the statement name, the invoice issuer and who holds customer data; it is not a setting on a payment integration.
A liability can be handed to a provider only by letting the provider become the seller to the customer, and only as far as the provider's contract says.
can_do: Decide for a stated business whether a merchant-of-record provider fits, and list what the business gives up.
Explain why a platform whose sellers are the merchants cannot solve its tax and dispute burden this way.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two businesses the chapter does not contain, the reader says which can use a merchant-of-record provider, what it gives up, and why the other cannot.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Business A is two people selling a €15-a-month note-taking app to consumers in 40 countries. Business B is a booking platform that takes payments for 500 independent hair salons. Which of them could put a merchant-of-record provider in front of its sales, what would it give up, and why can the other not?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A can: a fully automated digital product sold directly to customers. It gives up its own checkout and its name as seller on the statement and invoice, some control over refunds and disputes, part of the customer data, and pays a fee on top of payment fees. B cannot: the salons are the sellers of in-person services and the platform pays third parties, while a merchant of record must itself be the seller of what is sold.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can fill a three-column comparison of processor, payment facilitator and merchant of record for seller, statement name and tax liability.
acceptance_criteria.probe: For a processor, a payment facilitator (a provider that lets many businesses accept cards under its own agreement with the card networks) and a merchant of record: in each case, who is the seller to the buyer and who owes the sales tax or VAT?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Processor: the business is the seller and owes the tax. Payment facilitator: the business is still the seller and owes the tax. Merchant of record: the provider is the seller to the buyer and owes the tax, except where local rules prevent the transfer.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter's closing synthesizes the part around where the invoice lives, returns to Larkfield's 1 October and 1 November 2026 renewals, and hands off to Part VII through the fact that Larkfield's studios, not Larkfield, are the sellers.

The explanation of why Adyen has no merchant-of-record product is labeled as inference while Adyen's position is given as its own published statement, the Managed Payments release history is cited to Stripe's own pages, and no sentence says that the cost of disputes, refunds or reversals moves to the provider under Stripe's terms.

thesis.question: What changes when the provider, not you, is the merchant of record?
thesis.claim: When the provider is the merchant of record it sells your product to the customer in its own name, and only part of the seller's position moves with that. Under Stripe's Managed Payments, the one arrangement whose contract terms this chapter reads (as of November 2026), the provider's entity is the name on the customer's bank statement and the invoice, is the supplier for indirect tax wherever local rules let that transfer, and handles fraud screening, disputes and transaction support; the business remains the seller of record, books the revenue and pays the full cost of disputes, refunds and reversals, on top of a fee and the loss of control over the checkout, the eligible products and the integration. Because the provider must itself be the party the customer buys from, this is an operating model, not a feature added to a payment integration, and it does not fit a platform whose sellers are third parties: Managed Payments, in a release version of the API since 22 April 2026, takes digital products sold directly and excludes Connect platforms. Adyen states that it does not act as a merchant of record.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a merchant of record takes the seller's liabilities whole, the cost of fraud and disputes included, so that a business can switch it on as a compliance add-on to an existing integration; and the view that it is a payment facilitator under another name.
thesis.so_what: The reader can decide fit from the business model before reading a price list: a small seller of an automated digital product in many tax jurisdictions gains most, and a business that needs its own checkout, sells goods or human-delivered services, or pays other sellers is excluded or loses more than it gains. A business that adopts the model still budgets for lost disputes and refunds, and reads the provider's contract to see what moves. It also explains why Larkfield cannot hand its studios' tax and disputes to such a provider: the studios are the sellers.
thesis.how_why: Tax authorities and card networks hold the party that sells to the customer responsible, so a provider can take over the indirect tax and the name on the statement only by selling in its own name, and a party that sells in its own name decides what it sells and how. How much else moves is set by the provider's contract, not by the term. Stripe's service terms (last modified 28 September 2026) make its affiliate Sold through Link, LLC the merchant of record and the supplier 'for Indirect Tax purposes only', say that it 'is not the seller of record' and 'will not book the revenue', and keep the business liable 'for the full amount of any Disputes, refunds, and Reversals': Stripe handles a dispute and the business pays for it. The terms thus split two roles: merchant of record and tax supplier move to Stripe's affiliate, while seller of record and the revenue stay with the business. Stripe's documentation shows the other consequences: a fee of 3.5% on top of payment fees, the customer sees 'Sold through Link', only Checkout and Payment Links are supported, access depends on an eligibility review, and in some countries (Japan for domestic sales, for example) the tax liability does not transfer. Paddle sells the role as one bundled price and says it acts as the seller, and app stores are its older form. The release history is in Stripe's own pages: announced on 7 May 2025, in the preview API version 2026-02-25.preview, in the release version 2026-04-22.dahlia, and open to all digital businesses according to Stripe's blog of 29 April 2026; no page read uses the words 'generally available', and Apple's public developer agreement (Schedule 2, 13 October 2026) appoints Apple as agent or commissionaire depending on the region. Adyen's article of 15 September 2026 says that it 'doesn't act as a direct, third-party merchant of record'; that it offers no such product because its enterprise merchants are their own sellers in each market is the author's inference, not a documented reason.

role.contribution: Closes the part with the limiting case: instead of carrying the seller's obligations yourself, let the provider sell in its own name, and see which obligations move and which stay. It also carries the part's closing and sets up Part VII by showing a model that platforms cannot use.

transition_in.carries_over: The obligations chapters 27 to 31 left with the seller: running the billing engine, registering for and filing tax, answering disputes, and producing the data finance needs.
transition_in.introduces: A model that moves some of them (the indirect tax, the handling of fraud and disputes, the name on the statement) by changing who sells to the customer, and what that costs in money, control and customer data.

parts.title: Part VII — PLATFORMS: Paying Many Parties

know: The three questions every platform payment answers (who is the merchant, whose balance holds the money, who carries the loss) and where each provider records the answer: Stripe in an account's responsibilities and the charge type, Adyen in the account structure, the liable balance account and each payment's split instructions.
That seller verification is a state the provider reopens for the life of the account, and that payouts are usually the first thing to stop when a requirement passes its deadline.
How one payment is divided and paid out on each provider, and what happens to a refund or chargeback that arrives after the seller was paid.
Which accounts, cards and financing products each provider offers to a platform's sellers as of November 2026, at which release stage, and under which license.
believe: Choosing an account model is choosing who pays when a seller cannot; it is not an integration detail.
A platform that never holds funds can still carry the loss on them.
can_do: For a described platform business, say who the merchant is, which account and charge configuration follows on each provider, and whose balance a chargeback debits.
Design the platform's own records for sellers: the liability decisions per account, the verification requirements and deadlines, a ledger entry per leg of a split, and an exposure figure per seller.
Judge a proposal to add accounts, cards or financing by license, country, release stage and the duties it adds to the platform.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.
Given a platform business the part does not contain, a reader of Part VII alone says who carries a seller's unrecoverable chargebacks and names the earlier decision that settled it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A tutoring marketplace charges parents under its own name and pays tutors every Friday. One tutor collects €9,000 in prepaid lessons, is paid out, and disappears; the parents' banks reverse the payments (chargebacks). Using only Part VII: who ends up paying the €9,000, what decided that, and what number should the marketplace have been tracking?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The marketplace pays. Parents understand they are buying from the marketplace, so it is the merchant and the payments are booked through its own balance at the provider; chargebacks debit that balance (the platform balance on Stripe, the liable balance account on Adyen), and it can recover only what the tutor's balance or bank account still yields. The decision was the account and charge model chosen at the start, not anything done at dispute time. The number is exposure per seller: volume already paid out that can still be refunded or disputed.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of Part VII can list what a platform must check before offering sellers a card or a stored balance, without assuming the product is available wherever the platform takes payments.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A platform that takes payments in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the United States wants to give its sellers a debit card that spends their sales balance. Name the questions it must answer, per provider and per country, before it promises a launch date.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Which licensed institution issues the card and holds the balance (the provider's own bank license or a partner bank); whether the product is available in each country and at which release stage (generally available, preview, in development), with the date of that information; whether the platform's current account model qualifies (on Stripe, as documented, the platform must bear seller losses); what extra verification sellers must pass; and who answers each card authorization within the two-second window and what the default is when the platform does not answer.

thesis.question: What does a platform take on when it puts itself between a payer and a seller?
thesis.claim: A platform takes on its sellers' unpaid refunds, chargebacks and negative balances, and the work of keeping those sellers verified, to the extent its account model assigns them to it; it makes that assignment when it configures accounts and payments, long before the first loss, and not holding the funds does not undo it.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the account model is an integration and user-experience choice (which dashboard sellers see, how sign-up looks, which API calls are made), and that liability is a contract question legal can settle afterwards, since the provider holds the license and the money.
thesis.so_what: A platform team that accepts the claim decides who bears seller losses first and derives onboarding, the split and the product plan from that; it stops reading 'we never hold the funds' as 'we never carry the loss', and it keeps its own figure for how much paid-out money can still come back.
thesis.how_why: Card-network rules decide who the merchant is by what the cardholder sees and who gives recourse, and both providers turn that into configuration. Stripe's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) fixes an account's fee and loss responsibilities when it is configured as a merchant and does not let them be changed; negative transactions follow the charge type to the seller's or the platform's balance. Adyen's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) books everything to the platform's liable balance account unless split instructions say otherwise and debits that account when a seller's balance goes negative. The same assignment decides who collects verification data, where a refund after payout lands, and whether accounts and cards may be offered at all. Adyen documents an arrangement in which it bears seller losses only as a pilot with limited availability (Managed Risk), so on that point the comparison is between Stripe's standing per-account option and an Adyen pilot.

supporting_claims.claim: Who the customer understands they are buying from decides who the merchant is; the account and charge configuration must follow that fact, and it fixes whose balance refunds and chargebacks debit and who stands behind a seller's negative balance.

Seller verification is a state the provider reopens for as long as the account lives, and a platform that treats it as a sign-up form finds out through stopped payouts; who collects the data follows from who bears the losses.

A split is provisional because sellers are paid before the refund and dispute window closes: a reversal after payout is funded by the platform whenever the payment was booked through it, so the platform's exposure is the paid-out volume that can still come back.

Accounts, cards and financing for sellers reach only as far as a license or partner bank does, are offered at different release stages per country, and add duties to the platform; on Stripe, as documented, only a platform that already bears seller losses may offer accounts and cards.

role.contribution: Shows that the gap between the instant answer and the slow truth gets a third party to carry it once a platform sits between payer and seller, and that the platform chooses how much of it to carry when it picks its account model.

additional_patterns.applies_to: platform-onboarding-and-verification to embedded-finance: a seller is admitted, then paid, then offered more than payments

flow.rationale: The model chapter fixes who the merchant is and who bears losses. On Stripe that decision determines who collects verification data, so onboarding cannot be explained before it. A seller must hold an active capability before any payment can be split to it, so onboarding precedes splits. Embedded finance comes last because its products sit on the seller balance the splits chapter defines and, on Stripe, require the loss assignment the first chapter explains. If splits came first, the reader would watch a refund debit the platform's balance with no reason for it; if embedded finance came earlier, its preconditions would be terms the reader has not met.

hook.content: On 18 March 2027 Mila Janssen asks for €84.00 back for the seven classes she has not used on her €120 pass. Studio Noord was paid its €117.47 a week earlier, on Thursday 11 March. Mila will get her €84.00; the open question is whose balance it comes out of today, and that was decided long before she asked.

opening.bridge: From the two-party payments of Parts I to VI, where the business that takes the payment is the business that owes the refund, to a platform such as Larkfield, which is not the seller, never holds the money, and can still be the one that pays.
opening.roadmap: Four chapters in the order a platform meets the questions: who is the merchant and who carries the loss; how sellers are verified and kept verified; how one payment is divided, paid out and reversed; and what it takes to offer sellers accounts, cards and financing.

closing.synthesis: The four chapters describe one decision seen four times. Who stands behind a seller's negative balance decides who the provider lets collect verification data, where a refund after payout is booked, and whether the platform may offer accounts and cards at all. A platform that picks its account model for the look of its onboarding has picked its loss exposure, its operational workload and the limit of its product plan in the same act.
closing.so_what: Before adding sellers, countries or financial products, a platform can state its position in one line per provider: who is the merchant, who bears negative balances, who collects requirements, where reversals after payout are booked. If it cannot, it is carrying a liability it has not measured.
closing.callback: Mila's €84.00 refund a week after Studio Noord's payout: the reader can now say which balance funded it on each provider and why, and what Larkfield would need in place before letting studios spend that same balance on a card.

takeaway.content: Write down, per provider, the four answers (merchant, loss bearer, requirements collector, where reversals after payout are booked), mirror every seller's requirements and deadlines with an owner, and track exposure per seller, before launching any product that keeps or lends seller money.

transition_in.carries_over: Part VI's billing machinery and its last chapter's question of who sells to the customer, answered there by letting the provider sell in its own name (merchant of record).
transition_in.introduces: The opposite arrangement: the seller stays the seller, a platform stands between it and the payer, and the liability, of which a merchant of record takes over only the part its contract names, is now divided among three parties by the account model.

posts.title: Part VII — PLATFORMS: Paying Many Parties
posts.question: What does Part VII argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?

know: Part VII argues that a platform's account model is its liability model, and answers four questions in order: who is the merchant and who carries the loss, how sellers are verified, how a payment is divided and paid out, and what accounts, cards and financing require.
believe: A platform that never holds funds can still be the party that pays for a refund or a chargeback.
can_do: Pick the Part VII chapter that answers the platform decision in front of them.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can state the part's claim and name the four chapters' subjects in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what does Part VII argue, and what will each of its four chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The account model a platform chooses decides who pays when a seller cannot. Then: platform models (merchant, money, loss); onboarding and verification of sellers; splits, seller balances and payouts, including a refund after payout; accounts, cards and financing for sellers.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page opens with Mila's €84.00 refund request of 18 March 2027 after Studio Noord's payout of 11 March, with amounts and dates as in the scenario ledger, and leaves the question of who funds it open for the chapters.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: poses the refund-after-payout question, states the part thesis and gives the reading order.

posts.title: One Payment, Three Parties: Platform and Marketplace Models
posts.question: When a platform sits between payer and seller, who is the merchant, who holds the money and who carries the loss?

know: What a payment facilitator, a sponsored merchant and a marketplace are in card-network rules, and why most platforms use a provider's platform product instead of registering as a facilitator.

Stripe Connect's charge types and the responsibilities an account carries, and Adyen for Platforms' resources (legal entity, account holder, balance account, liable balance account), as answers to the same three questions.

What each provider documents about negative seller balances, and that Adyen documents the platform as the default bearer, a 30-day negative-balance period, and a Managed Risk pilot in which Adyen bears seller losses.
believe: Who bears seller losses is the first decision of a platform integration, because the other settings depend on it and on Stripe it cannot be changed on an existing account.
can_do: Given a platform business, name the merchant from what the customer sees, choose the matching configuration on each provider, and say whose balance a chargeback debits and who stands behind it.
Translate a statement made in one provider's platform vocabulary into the other's, and say where the two do not map one to one.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a platform business the chapter does not contain, the reader identifies the merchant from what the customer sees, not from the API calls, and derives the configuration and the loss bearer on both providers.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A booking tool for dog groomers lets a customer book and pay a named groomer; the groomer's name is on the card statement and the tool keeps 3%. Using only this chapter: who is the merchant, which kind of charge or account setup fits on Stripe and on Adyen, and if a customer's bank reverses a payment (a chargeback) after the groomer has closed the business, who pays?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The groomer is the merchant, because the customer understands they are buying from the groomer. On Stripe that means a direct charge, or a charge through the platform that names the groomer as the business of record; on Adyen the platform model, in which the shopper deals directly with the platform's user. The chargeback debits the groomer's balance on a Stripe direct charge, and if that balance stays negative the loss goes to whoever was assigned negative-balance responsibility when the account was configured (Stripe or the tool). On Adyen it debits the tool's liable balance account by default unless the payment's chargeback instructions name the groomer's balance account, and by default the liable account stands behind a negative seller balance (Adyen's Managed Risk pilot is the documented exception).

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every Stripe and Adyen statement about liability carries its source and date, and the chapter says in plain words that Adyen's default puts the platform behind its sellers and that Adyen bearing seller losses is documented only as a pilot with limited availability (Managed Risk).

The terms the rest of Part VII relies on (connected account, charge type, balance platform, account holder, balance account, liable account, negative balance) are each defined here in one sentence before they are used.

thesis.question: When a platform sits between payer and seller, who is the merchant, who holds the money and who carries the loss?
thesis.claim: The merchant is whoever the customer understands they are buying from, the money sits in balances at the provider and not with the platform, and the loss falls first on the balance the payment was booked to and then on the party assigned to cover that balance when it goes negative. The platform's configuration does not decide who the merchant is, but it must agree with it, and it does decide the booking and the loss bearer, on Stripe permanently for each account.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that Standard, Express and Custom accounts, or marketplace and platform setups, differ in how much user interface the platform builds, so the choice belongs to the product team and can be revisited when the business model changes.
thesis.so_what: A team should settle who bears seller losses before it designs onboarding or the checkout, record that decision per account in its own systems, and expect a change of commercial model on Stripe to mean new accounts for its sellers, not a changed setting.
thesis.how_why: Visa's rules (October 2026 edition) classify an entity as the merchant if it sells to the cardholder, is named to the cardholder and gives recourse in a dispute. Stripe's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) tells platforms to determine the merchant of record from the business model and not from the charge type, books negative transactions to the seller's balance for direct charges and to the platform's for charges made through the platform, offers a setting under which Stripe is responsible for negative seller balances, and says of an account's fee and loss responsibilities that their values cannot be updated later. Adyen's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) books amounts and fees to the platform's liable balance account unless split instructions say otherwise and deducts from it when sellers' balance accounts go negative. Where they differ, as documented in 2026: Stripe exposes loss bearing as a per-account choice with Stripe as one option; Adyen puts the platform behind its sellers by default and documents, as a pilot with limited availability, a Managed Risk programme in which Adyen bears seller losses.

role.contribution: Establishes the three questions, the two vocabularies and the loss assignment that the other three chapters build on.

transition_in.carries_over: The part intro's open question: Studio Noord has been paid, Mila wants €84.00 back, and someone's balance must fund it.
transition_in.introduces: The answer in general form: who the merchant is, whose balance holds the money and who stands behind that balance, stated in Stripe's and in Adyen's terms.

posts.title: Letting Sellers In: Onboarding and Verification on Platforms
posts.question: How does a platform get thousands of small businesses verified without losing them or its licence partner's trust?

know: What a capability and a verification requirement are, and how each provider reports what is missing and by when: Stripe as lists of requirements with a per-account deadline, Adyen as a per-capability allowed flag with standard deadlines of 30 or 60 days.
The events that reopen verification after sign-up: changed seller data, changed rules, volume thresholds and periodic reviews.
The three ways to collect verification data (provider-hosted, embedded components, the platform's own forms over the API) and what each leaves the platform to maintain.
That neither company publishes a completion rate or a comparison of its onboarding flows; the one public figure is a 2019 Stripe claim about a redesign.
believe: Verification is a state with deadlines and an owner, not a form completed once.
Collecting sellers' documents itself is work a platform should take on only when it has also chosen to carry their losses.
can_do: Diagnose a seller's stopped payouts from requirement and capability state, and say what the platform should have stored and surfaced to prevent it.
Choose between hosted, embedded and API onboarding for a stated platform, naming what the platform must then keep up to date.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a seller complaint the chapter does not contain, the reader explains it from verification state and names the records and the owner that would have prevented it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A seller on your platform writes: 'Customers can still pay me, but my payouts stopped on Monday and nobody told me why.' Using only this chapter: what most likely happened, why did payouts stop while payments continued, and what should the platform have had in place?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A verification requirement was reopened (changed data, a new rule, a threshold or a periodic review) and its deadline passed. Payouts go first: Stripe documents that it typically disables payouts at the deadline and charges only later, and Adyen's standard deadline is 30 days for payout capabilities against 60 for receiving payments. The platform should mirror each seller's open requirements, deadlines and capability status from the provider, give every deadline an owner, remind the seller through a monitored channel, and show the seller the reason and the provider's link or component to fix it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a proposal to build onboarding forms on the API, the reader names what the platform takes on that a hosted flow would have carried.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your product team wants its own sign-up forms for sellers, sending the data to the provider by API, to keep the brand consistent. Using only this chapter, name two things the platform takes on by doing so.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Any two of: keeping the forms current when requirements change (Stripe documents that API onboarding needs integration changes and a review at least every six months, while hosted and embedded flows update immediately); handling sellers' identity documents itself; supporting each new country and business type by hand; and, on Stripe, a configuration in which the platform collects requirements only if it also bears seller losses.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter states that no completion rate or comparison of onboarding flows is public for either provider, and presents the one published figure (Stripe, 2019) as a dated vendor claim.

thesis.question: How does a platform get thousands of small businesses verified without losing them or its licence partner's trust?
thesis.claim: By treating verification as a state the provider reopens for the life of every account, not as a sign-up step. To keep sellers, the platform requests only the capabilities a seller needs and lets the provider's hosted or embedded flow collect the documents; to keep the trust of the licensed provider, whose license requires the checks, it mirrors every open requirement and deadline with a named owner, so that the seller hears of a missing document from the platform first and the provider does not have to restrict an account the platform had not noticed.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that onboarding is a conversion funnel that ends at sign-up, so the platform should own every screen through the API to keep drop-off low, and can leave what happens afterwards to the provider's emails to the seller.
thesis.so_what: Verification becomes an operated system with an owner, alerts and a seller-facing explanation, not a project that ends at launch: the first thing a neglected requirement breaks is a seller's payout, the first place it shows is the support queue, and because neither provider publishes a completion rate or a comparison of flows the platform has to measure sign-up drop-off on its own flows.
thesis.how_why: Both providers gate what a seller may do behind capabilities that depend on verification, and both reopen verification after sign-up. Adyen's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) names the events that trigger verification, among them a seller changing its data and periodic data reviews, and standard deadlines of 30 days for payout capabilities and 60 for receiving payments; Stripe's (n.d., accessed November 2026) lists requirements as currently due, eventually due and past due against a per-account deadline and says it typically disables payouts first. That is the documented difference: Adyen's deadlines are standard periods a platform can build reminders on, Stripe's must be read per account. Stripe also documents that its hosted and embedded flows pick up new requirements immediately while API onboarding needs integration changes, and that who collects requirements is derived from who bears losses. Neither company publishes a completion rate or a comparison of its flows, so the cost of a hosted flow in lost sign-ups cannot be stated from the public record.

role.contribution: Shows the first consequence of the loss assignment: the provider's license requires every seller to be verified continuously, and the platform inherits the deadlines whether or not it collects the data.

transition_in.carries_over: Chapter 33's result that every seller is an account at a licensed provider, with someone standing behind its losses.
transition_in.introduces: What follows from that: the provider must know who each seller is before the account may take payments or receive payouts, and must keep knowing it, which makes verification a state with deadlines.

posts.title: Dividing the Money: Splits, Platform Balances and Seller Payouts
posts.question: How is one payment divided among platform, seller and provider, and how does each get paid?

know: How a payment is divided on each provider: on Stripe an application fee or later transfers between balances, depending on the charge type; on Adyen a list of typed split instructions sent with the payment or applied from a store's profile.
Who pays the processing fee in each setup, and why on Adyen some fees are not known when the payment is made.
What a refund and a chargeback do to a payment that was already split and paid out, and the tools for recovering the seller's share.
How seller payouts are scheduled on each provider and what a top-up is.
believe: A split is not final when the seller is paid; it is final when the payment can no longer be refunded or disputed.
'Payment succeeded' does not prove 'seller credited'; only reconciling each leg does.
can_do: Write the ledger entries for one split payment, its payout and a later refund, keyed so the refund finds the bookings it must unwind.
Say, for a refund or chargeback after payout, whose balance is debited first and how the platform recovers the seller's share.
Compute a per-seller exposure figure from paid-out volume and the refund and dispute windows.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a split payment the chapter does not contain, refunded after the seller was paid, the reader says who is out of pocket if the seller cannot repay and what record the platform needed in order to unwind the split.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A marketplace charges a buyer €200 through its own account at the provider, keeps €20 and credits the seller €180, which is paid out to the seller's bank on Friday. On Monday the buyer is refunded in full. The seller's balance at the provider is empty and the seller does not answer. Using only this chapter: who has paid for the refund so far, how can the marketplace try to get the €180 back, and what must it have recorded on Friday to do so?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The marketplace has paid: the refund debits the balance the payment was booked through (the platform balance on Stripe, the liable balance account on Adyen, which also stands behind a seller balance that goes negative). It can reverse the seller's share so that the seller's balance turns negative and is refilled from future sales, or debit the seller's bank account where the seller consented. It needed a record linking the charge to each leg of the split (seller share, platform fee, provider fee, payout), so that the refund can find what to reverse.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can explain why an approved payment on Adyen does not prove that the seller was credited, and name what to reconcile.
acceptance_criteria.probe: On Adyen, a payment with split instructions is approved. Using only this chapter: can the platform conclude that the seller's balance account was credited? Why or why not, and what should it check?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No. Adyen documents that the payment request validates only the format of the split instructions; if the named balance account does not exist or its account holder is closed, the whole amount and its fees are booked to the platform's liable balance account without an error. The platform should reconcile the bookings per split (transfer webhooks or the accounting report) against its own ledger.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The worked example splits Mila's €120.00 into €117.47 for Studio Noord and a €2.53 Larkfield fee, with the €0.61 provider cost labeled as an assumption, and the refund of €84.00 on 18 March 2027 follows the payout of 11 March, all as in the scenario ledger.

thesis.question: How is one payment divided among platform, seller and provider, and how does each get paid?
thesis.claim: A payment is divided by booking parts of it to balances inside the provider: the seller's share to the seller's balance, the platform's fee to the platform's, and the provider's fee deducted from whichever of the two the configuration names; seller and platform are then paid by later payouts from their balances. Because sellers are paid before the refund and dispute window closes, the division is provisional: a refund or chargeback after payout is funded by the platform whenever the payment was booked through it, and the platform must then recover the seller's share itself.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a split is arithmetic done once at payment time (compute the fee, send the rest), that a refund runs the same arithmetic backwards, and that the provider keeps the parties square.
thesis.so_what: The platform needs a ledger entry for every leg of a split, keyed so a refund can find what to reverse, a per-seller figure for paid-out volume that can still come back, and a reconciliation that checks each seller was credited; a platform that only tracks 'paid' discovers the shortfall later, as an unexplained difference between its own ledger and the provider's balances.
thesis.how_why: On Stripe the division is a set of movements between the platform's and the seller's balances that follows the charge type; on Adyen it is a list of typed split instructions declared with the payment. Stripe's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) moves the full amount of a destination charge to the seller and the application fee back to the platform, debits the platform's balance for a refund or dispute on a charge made through the platform, and leaves recovery to a transfer reversal the platform requests; a direct charge debits the seller's balance instead. Adyen's (n.d., accessed November 2026) takes a splits list with types for the seller's share, the commission and each fee, calculates transaction fees after the payment, allows a refund to be deducted only from the balance accounts that were credited, and has the platform choose where a chargeback will be booked when it sends the payment. Two documented differences matter to an integrator: Adyen fixes the chargeback booking at payment time where Stripe leaves the reversal to dispute time, and a split naming a missing or closed balance account is booked to the liable account without an error on Adyen, where a Stripe transfer fails. Each company has published a general account of its internal ledger; how either books a platform's splits and transfers in it is not public.

role.contribution: Turns the loss assignment into money movements: shows where each euro of a payment is booked, when it leaves the provider, and whose balance funds a reversal that arrives afterwards.

transition_in.carries_over: A verified seller whose capabilities to receive payments and payouts are active.
transition_in.introduces: The first payment to that seller: how it is divided among three parties, when each is paid, and what a reversal after payout does to the division.

posts.title: Beyond Payments: Accounts, Cards and Capital as Platform Features
posts.question: What does it take to offer accounts, cards and loans to a platform's sellers, and how far have the two providers gone?

know: What banking-as-a-service, a financial account, card issuing and financing repaid from processed volume are, in plain words.
Which license stands behind each product: Adyen's own banking licenses, and Stripe's money-transmission and e-money licenses with named partner banks and lenders.
The stated availability of each product as of November 2026, by country and release stage, including what is in preview or in development.
That issuing puts the platform in the card authorization path with a two-second window on both providers.
believe: Embedded finance is not switched on where payments already run; it is a separate decision per product, per country and per release stage.
Each product that keeps, spends or lends seller money adds duties to the platform even though the provider holds the license.
can_do: Assess a proposal to offer sellers an account, a card or financing by license, country, release stage, preconditions on the platform's account model and the duties added.
State what happens to card payments when the platform's authorization endpoint does not answer, and choose the default deliberately.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a product plan the chapter does not contain, the reader lists the checks to make per provider and per country and treats the chapter's availability facts as dated.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A platform with sellers in Germany and the United States wants to let them keep their sales in an account at the provider instead of being paid out to their bank, starting next quarter. Using only this chapter: what must it check on Stripe and on Adyen before promising that date, and what would you say about how current the chapter's own answer is?
acceptance_criteria.expected: On each provider: whether an account product for platform users is available in each country and at which stage (as of November 2026, Stripe's current platform product was in preview, with a US legacy version not open to new builds, and Adyen described business accounts as in development); which licensed institution holds the funds; the preconditions (on Stripe the platform must bear seller losses; on Adyen the feature is enabled per balance platform, with extra verification and Adyen's authentication SDK for outgoing transfers); and what the platform must now run (statements, authentication, fraud controls). The reader adds that these stages are dated November 2026 and must be checked again.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader can say what a provider does when the platform does not answer a card authorization in time.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your platform issues cards to sellers and approves each purchase from its own server. That server is unreachable for ten minutes. Using only this chapter: what happens to purchases made on those cards during that time?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Each authorization waits up to two seconds for the platform's answer (2 seconds on Stripe, 2,000 milliseconds on Adyen, as documented); with no answer the provider applies the default the platform configured in advance, approve or decline. The platform therefore decided the outcome when it set the default, and its endpoint needs its own availability target.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every availability statement names its release stage and country and is dated; nothing in preview, pilot or development is described as available.

The chapter's conclusion synthesizes Part VII (one loss assignment seen in the model, verification, the split and financial products) and returns to Mila's €84.00 refund after payout before handing off to Part VIII.

thesis.question: What does it take to offer accounts, cards and loans to a platform's sellers, and how far have the two providers gone?
thesis.claim: It takes a licensed institution behind each product, and that license covers the product, not the platform's operating duties: the platform must answer each card authorization within two seconds and accept what the provider attaches, which is added seller verification on Adyen and bearing seller losses on Stripe. Neither provider has reached a feature switch: as of November 2026 availability differs by product, country and release stage, and accounts for a platform's sellers are in preview at Stripe and in development at Adyen.
thesis.disputed_by: The view, encouraged by provider descriptions such as Adyen's 'within a single integration' (H1 2026 shareholder letter), that a platform already taking payments can add accounts, cards and loans as features wherever it operates, with the provider carrying the regulated part.
thesis.so_what: A platform plans these products per country and per release stage, checks whether its account model qualifies before it promises anything, and treats a card or account launch as taking on operating duties of a financial product; declining to launch, as Larkfield, the book's fictional platform, does with its instant-payout card, is a legitimate result of that assessment.
thesis.how_why: Adyen's H1 2026 shareholder letter attributes its accounts, issuing and capital products to its own banking licenses, and its statements carry merchant funds in business accounts and loans on its own balance sheet. Stripe's documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026) says Stripe is not a bank and names partner banks for deposits, cards and loans and third-party lenders outside the United States. That is the documented difference: one licensed balance sheet extended across products, against products assembled per country from partners. On Stripe a platform for which Stripe bears seller losses cannot use Treasury or Issuing, which ties these products to the loss assignment of chapter 33; on Adyen they are enabled per balance platform with added capabilities and verification. Both give the platform about two seconds to approve a card authorization before a configured default applies. As of November 2026 both offer card issuing and financing in named countries; Stripe's current account product for platforms is in public preview in the United Kingdom and private preview in the United States, Australia and the EU (and, on one page, Canada), with a US legacy version closed to new builds, and Adyen's business accounts are documented as in development. The public record gives no date for general availability of either company's account product, so the chapter reports stages as of November 2026 and stops there.

role.contribution: Tests the part's claim at its far end: the products built on the seller balance are gated by license and by the platform's loss assignment; also carries the part's closing.

transition_in.carries_over: The seller balance of chapter 35, which exists between the split and the payout and is emptied on a schedule.
transition_in.introduces: What a platform can offer if that money stays, is spent or is advanced (an account, a card, financing), and what each requires of the provider's license and of the platform.

parts.title: Part VIII — SCALE: Reliability, Data and Operations

know: What Stripe and Adyen have each published, with dates, about availability targets and contracts, incidents, databases and sharding, hosting, peak figures, rate limits and rollout practice.

Where the public record stops for both companies: the topology and timing of a failover between data centers or regions, cells, which data is replicated synchronously and the design of the webhook sender; and what is published short of that (Adyen lists its data centers by continent or country and states that its load balancers fail over between them; Stripe names no AWS region).

The vocabulary of operating a money path: availability target, failure isolation, graceful degradation, shard, consistency boundary, outbox, data residency and localization, backpressure, progressive rollout, dark launch.
believe: A payment that is late can be repaired with an apology; a payment that is wrong costs refunds, disputes and trust, so a money path is designed to be late before it is wrong.
A provider's reliability cannot be read from its uptime figure, and a statement about its regions or failover that carries no source is a guess.
can_do: For a money-moving path in their own system, say what gives way under a dependency failure, a peak and a change (what lags, what is refused, what is paced, what is rolled back) and show that the record of money is not on that list.
Sort a statement about how Stripe or Adyen runs its infrastructure into documented with a year, partially documented, or not public.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is argued by at least one chapter, and every chapter supports at least one.
Each chapter's closing hand-off expresses the relationship its successor declares in transition_in.

Given a design choice between making a payment late and risking making it wrong, in a case the part does not contain, a reader of Part VIII chooses late and names the mechanism that keeps the late payment from being lost.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A ticket seller's payment provider slows down during a sale. The seller can either (a) hold checkout requests in a queue for up to a minute, or (b) give up after five seconds, show 'payment failed' and let the customer press pay again, which sends a new request. Using Part VIII: which is safer for the money, and what must be true for the other option to be acceptable?
acceptance_criteria.expected: (a): a late answer can be repaired, a double charge cannot be undone without a refund. (b) is acceptable only if the retry carries the same idempotency key (a key that makes the provider treat the second request as the first) and the seller fetches the provider's record before telling the customer the payment failed, because a timeout is an unknown outcome, not a failure.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given statements about the two providers' infrastructure, a reader of Part VIII separates the documented ones from the ones the public record does not support.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Mark each as documented, partially documented or not public, as of November 2026: (1) Stripe runs on Amazon Web Services. (2) Adyen runs in its own data centers. (3) Stripe serves its API from several regions at once. (4) Adyen's contract promises 99.9% uptime per quarter. (5) Adyen can move a merchant's traffic from one region to another within seconds. (6) Stripe deploys to a core API service about 400 times a day.
acceptance_criteria.expected: (1) documented (2023, 2024, current documentation); (2) documented (2021, 2025, 2026), with a list of sites by continent or country and no cities or count beyond 'tens of data centres'; (3) not public; (4) documented in the public terms (last updated 1 November 2023) as a 'commercially reasonable efforts' clause, with exclusions; (5) partially documented: Adyen's documentation says its load balancers 'manage the failover to the other data centers' and mentions 'alternative routing' to 'backup infrastructure', with no timing or topology, so 'within seconds' is not public; (6) documented in the 2023 annual letter, published 2024.

thesis.question: How is a system that moves money kept running through failures, growth, legal limits on where data may live, peaks and constant change, and how much of Stripe's and Adyen's answer is public?
thesis.claim: A payment platform is run at scale by deciding in advance what gives way (the freshness of the books under failure, a system-wide transaction under growth, a global identifier under a localization law, a caller's burst under peak, the reach of a rollout under change), and in every design Stripe or Adyen has published the record of money is not among the things relaxed; the two have documented their choices on outages, data stores, limits and rollouts, and neither has published a cell design or the topology or timing of a failover of its payment path between its data centers or regions.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that scale in payments is ordinary web scale with a stricter number: add redundancy and capacity until the uptime figure is reached, keep everything strongly consistent everywhere, and treat availability as the first measure of a provider.
thesis.so_what: A team that accepts the claim writes down, for each of its own money-moving paths, what is allowed to lag, be refused, be paced or be rolled back, and stops comparing providers by a count of nines or by an assumed failover design that neither provider has documented.
thesis.how_why: Something has to give when a dependency fails, data outgrows one database, a law fixes where data sits, a month's renewals arrive in six hours or a change goes wrong. The published designs show what was chosen: Adyen's 2021 account lets accounting run behind so the edge keeps answering; Stripe's 2017 account sheds non-critical requests first and its 2024 account moves data between shards with a write pause of under two seconds that retries absorb; Stripe's India page (updated 2023) records features cut to keep data in the country; Stripe's documented limits (accessed November 2026) cap each account long before capacity; Stripe's 2023 annual letter stages every change by traffic share. In none of them is the record of money the thing that is relaxed. On the topology and timing of failover, on cells and on which data is replicated synchronously the public record of both companies stops (Adyen lists its data centers by continent or country and states that its load balancers fail over between them; Stripe names no AWS region and describes takeover only for billing usage events, not for payments), and the part says so instead of inferring.

supporting_claims.claim: A payment path stays available because its operator decides beforehand what may lag or be shed, and the lasting cost of an outage is the payments left with an unknown outcome, which published uptime figures do not report.

Once money data is split across shards or clusters, it is kept consistent by small local transactions, idempotent retries, messages between clusters and verification afterwards, not by a transaction that spans the system.

Where payment data lives is settled by localization law where one applies and by the provider's hosting model elsewhere, before any engineering goal, and the public record gives each provider's hosting, the regions Adyen names and what each has said about India, but not the topology or timing of a failover.
A merchant's predictable peak fails at the provider's per-customer limits, not at the provider's capacity, so the load has to be paced by the party that creates it.
Change on a money path is made safe by bounding how much live traffic a mistake can reach and testing the way back, and a change is finished only when the records agree after it.

role.contribution: Shows that the mechanisms of Parts II to VII keep their guarantees under failure, growth, peaks and change only because correctness is put ahead of availability, and fixes the limit of what can be said about either company's infrastructure before the journeys and the company cases rely on it.

additional_patterns.applies_to: payment-peak-load to payment-safe-change: the system that cannot be stopped for a peak, then how it is changed while running

flow.rationale: Reliability comes first because it introduces the split the other chapters use: a path that must answer and a record that must be right. Data stores then show how the record stays right once it is spread over shards; regions take the same shards and ask where they are allowed to be, and introduce the hosting difference (rented cloud, owned data centers) that the peak chapter needs to explain how each company gets capacity. Change comes last because the incidents the first four chapters cite (Stripe in July 2019 and February 2024, Adyen's partition near miss before a December peak) were all set off by a change, so the reader meets the cause after seeing its effects. Putting safe change first would discuss rollouts before the reader knows which path must answer and which record must be right; putting regions before data stores would ask where shards may live before saying what a shard is. Three of the five transitions are not sequence or support: the order is an argument from what must hold (the record) to what threatens it (growth, law, load, change).

hook.content: On 1 October 2026 Larkfield's renewal job hit its provider's rate limit and 7,900 membership renewals were delayed to the next day; dunning emails went to members who had done nothing wrong. On 1 November 2026 a provider call timed out, the job retried with a new idempotency key, and 1,840 members were charged twice: €71,300 refunded, and 212 disputes anyway. The first month was late. The second was wrong.

opening.bridge: From the engineer's habit of counting downtime as the cost of failure to the two Larkfield months, where the late run cost emails and the wrong run cost refunds and disputes: in a money path the order of priorities is the reverse of a content site's.
opening.roadmap: Five chapters, each naming what gives way so that the record does not: how a payment path stays up and what an outage leaves behind; which databases hold the money and how they stay consistent when split; where the systems and the data are allowed to live, a short chapter because little is public; how a predictable peak is met; and how a system that cannot stop is changed.

closing.synthesis: Read together, the five chapters show one asymmetry. What the two providers have documented is what they let give way: lagging books, a write pause of seconds, features cut in one country, a per-account limit, a rollout withdrawn at one percent. What neither has documented (the topology and timing of a failover, cells, which data is replicated synchronously) is the part a merchant cannot verify. A merchant's own reliability therefore rests on three things it can check: the contract, the documented limits, and its own measurement and reconciliation.
closing.so_what: The reader plans against the provider's contractual commitment and documented limits, measures payment success on their own side, and treats every outage, peak and deployment as finished only when the records agree, which is the same test the book applies to a single payment.
closing.callback: The two first-of-month runs from the part opening: 7,900 renewals a day late in October 2026, 1,840 members charged twice in November 2026. Keel's K5 accepts lateness on purpose by pacing renewals over 18 hours, and K1 removes the wrong outcome by deriving the key from the membership, the billing period and the number of the scheduled attempt.

takeaway.content: For each path in your system that moves money, write one line: when the provider is slow, at peak, and during a deploy, what gives way, and which check proves afterwards that the record did not.

transition_in.carries_over: From Part VII: the last of the mechanisms, a platform's account model, which decides who is liable for each seller's balance; and with it the full set of mechanisms from Parts II to VII, each described for one payment at a time.
transition_in.introduces: The same mechanisms under conditions no single payment shows: a dependency failing, data outgrowing one database, a law on where data sits, a month of renewals arriving in six hours, and several hundred deployments a day.

posts.title: Part VIII — SCALE: Reliability, Data and Operations
posts.question: What does Part VIII argue, and in what order should its chapters be read?

know: Part VIII answers five questions in order: how a payment path stays up, how its data stays consistent when split, where systems and data may live, how a peak is met, and how the system is changed while running.
This is the part of the book with the least public evidence, and chapter 39 is short for that reason.
believe: In a money path, late is cheaper than wrong.
can_do: Pick the Part VIII chapter that answers the operational question in front of them.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can name the five chapters' subjects in reading order and state the part's claim in one sentence.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what does Part VIII argue, and what will each of the next five chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: At scale something must give way, and in a payment system it is never the record of money; then reliability and outages, data stores and consistency, regions and data residency (short, little is public), peak load, safe change.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page opens on the two Larkfield first-of-month runs with the ledger's figures and says which was late and which was wrong.

The page tells the reader, before any chapter, that a cell design, the topology and timing of a failover between regions, which data is replicated synchronously and the webhook sender are not public for either company.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: the two Larkfield months, the part thesis, the reading order and the warning about where the evidence is thin.

posts.title: Down Is Not an Option: Reliability and Availability
posts.question: How do payment providers stay up, and what happens when they do not?

know: The different things published under the word 'uptime' by the two providers (a target, an achieved yearly figure, a peak-weekend figure, rolling 30-day and 90-day figures, a contractual commitment) and why they cannot be compared.

What failure isolation and graceful degradation mean in a payment path, and the two documented examples: accounting that runs behind the edge (Adyen, 2021) and shedding of non-critical requests (Stripe, 2017).
What the public incident accounts contain: Stripe's root-cause analysis of 10 July 2019 and its paragraph on 8 February 2024, Adyen's update on the attack of 21 April 2025 and its follow-up.
believe: An outage is not over when the status page recovers; it is over when every payment attempted during it has a known outcome.
The contractual commitment and its exclusions, not the reported figure, is the number to plan against.
can_do: Read a provider's availability figure and say what it measures, over what period, and what it leaves out.
For their own payment path, list which steps may be skipped, queued or refused when a dependency fails, and which may not.
After a provider outage, find the payments with unknown outcomes and resolve them without charging anyone twice.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a provider's reported and contracted availability and a described outage, the reader says which number to plan against and what to do about payments that timed out.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A provider's status page shows 99.999% for the last 30 days; its contract promises 99.9% per quarter, excluding failures at banks and card networks. Last month your checkout saw 40 minutes of failed and timed-out payments. Which number do you plan against, what do you measure yourself, and what do you do about the payments that timed out?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Plan against the contractual figure with its exclusions; measure payment success on your own side, because failures at banks and networks count against neither number; treat each timeout as an unknown outcome: fetch the provider's record or retry with the same idempotency key, and do not mark the payment failed or charge again until the record says so.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a payment path with a failing dependency the chapter does not discuss, the reader says whether the step should fail open, fail closed or be queued, and what that choice risks.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Your service that sends payment receipts by email is down, and so is the service that checks whether a studio is still allowed to take payments. For each: should the payment go ahead, be refused, or wait? Say what each choice risks.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Receipts: go ahead and queue the email; it can be late without money being wrong. The permission check: this decides whether money may move at all, so refusing or holding is defensible; letting it through (failing open) trades a compliance and loss risk for availability and must be a deliberate, written decision. The reader names the trade in both cases.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every availability figure in the chapter carries its publisher, its definition as published (or the statement that none is given) and its date, and the chapter says that no public service-level percentage for Stripe was found and that neither company publishes its failover design.
The terms availability target, failure isolation, graceful degradation and incident report are defined before they are used.

thesis.question: How do payment providers stay up, and what happens when they do not?
thesis.claim: A payment path is kept answering by an operator that has decided beforehand what may lag or be dropped (the books, the non-critical requests) so that no payment is recorded twice or lost; when the path fails anyway, the provider restores service and publishes little about it, and what the merchant has to repair is the set of payments whose outcome nobody knows, not the minutes of downtime.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that availability is a number to buy: pick the provider that reports the most nines, add redundancy on your own side, and consider an outage over when the status page says so.
thesis.so_what: The reader plans against the contractual commitment and its exclusions, measures payment success on their own side, and builds the sweep that resolves unknown outcomes before building a second provider connection.
thesis.how_why: Adyen described the split in 2021: for the edge 'the priority was uptime', while for accounting 'we don't mind if they are down for a little bit as long as we can guarantee their reliability and consistency', with a local database queue between them. Stripe described a different lever in 2017, reserving capacity for critical methods such as creating charges and shedding the rest, and committed to per-shard isolation after its outage of 10 July 2019; it has not published where state sits on its API path. The published figures do not settle a comparison: Stripe states a target of 99.9995% (2024, 2026) with no formula, and no public service-level percentage for Stripe was found; Adyen's public terms (last updated 1 November 2023) commit it to 'commercially reasonable efforts' toward 99.9% per quarter, with exclusions, while its status page reports successful requests over 30 days and Stripe's status page displays 99.999% over 90 days with no definition. None of these figures says what happened to requests that timed out. Stripe's root-cause analysis of 10 July 2019, the one full public account of an outage found, reports two windows of 27 and 93 minutes in which 'a substantial majority of API requests' failed, and says Stripe emailed every user with five or more failed POST requests: the cleanup was counted in requests, per customer, not in minutes. Neither company publishes its failover design or routine postmortems, and the chapter stops there.

role.contribution: Introduces the split between the path that must answer and the record that must be right, which every later chapter of the part uses, and replaces the uptime figure with the unknown-outcome payment as the measure of an outage.

transition_in.carries_over: The part opening's two first-of-month runs and its claim that something must give way so the record does not.
transition_in.introduces: The first thing that gives way: under failure, the freshness of the books and the non-critical requests, and what a merchant is left to repair afterwards.

posts.title: Never Lose a Cent: Data Stores and Consistency
posts.question: Which databases sit under a payment platform, and how do they keep money consistent while scaling?

know: What Stripe has published about its document database platform (2024, 2026) and its online migrations (2017), and what Adyen has published about PostgreSQL, its sharded accounting clusters (2021) and partitioning (2023 to 2025).
The terms shard, online migration, consistency boundary and outbox.
What is not public for either company: which data is replicated synchronously, read consistency, and how a transfer across shards or clusters is made atomic.
believe: The choice of database product matters less for money than where the consistency boundary is drawn and whether everything that crosses it is idempotent and checked afterwards.
can_do: Draw the consistency boundary for a payment record in their own system and say what is allowed to catch up later.
Replace a proposed cross-system transaction with a local transaction, an outbox and an idempotent consumer, and name the check that proves the two sides agree.
Plan the steps of an online migration of a payment table.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a proposal for a transaction across a database and a queue, the reader gives the outbox design and the duty it puts on the consumer.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A team must mark a payment as paid in its database and tell the booking system so that a class pass is activated. They propose one distributed transaction across the database and the message queue. What does this chapter suggest instead, what can still go wrong, and how is it caught?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Write the payment state and an outbox row in one local transaction; a separate process publishes the row, possibly more than once; the booking system deduplicates by event or payment id so that a repeat has no effect; a periodic comparison of paid payments against activated passes catches anything that was never delivered.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a design in which one account's money can sit in two shards, the reader identifies that a transfer between them is no longer one transaction and says what keeps it correct.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A ledger is split into four databases and new entries go to whichever database is next in turn. A payout must debit a balance whose entries are spread across two of them. Why is this harder than before the split, and what did Adyen say it did about it in 2021?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The debit can no longer be one local transaction; money has to be moved from one cluster to the other. Adyen's 2021 account says the migration was 'quite painful' and that jobs exchange 'back and forth messages between the clusters to keep everything aligned'; the protocol itself is not public. The reader adds that such messages must be idempotent and verified.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The statement that neither company uses a transaction spanning its money path is presented as an inference from the published mechanisms, labeled as such, and the chapter lists what is not public for each company.
Published scale figures for the two companies are given with their year and unit and are not ranked against each other.

thesis.question: Which databases sit under a payment platform, and how do they keep money consistent while scaling?
thesis.claim: Stripe scaled a document database and Adyen a relational one, and in what either has published no transaction spans the shards: the published mechanisms imply that money is kept consistent by local transactions, retries that are safe to repeat, messages between clusters and verification afterwards.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that money needs one strongly consistent relational database, or distributed transactions across every service that touches it, and that a document store or any eventual consistency has no place near a payment.
thesis.so_what: The reader stops asking which database is safe for money and instead draws a small consistency boundary (for Larkfield, the payment record and its outbox row), makes everything that crosses it idempotent, and adds a check that proves both sides agree.
thesis.how_why: Stripe's 2024 account describes DocDB, built on MongoDB Community, with more than 2,000 shards and a platform that moves data between them; during the switch, which takes under two seconds, 'all failed reads and writes directed to the source shard succeed on retries'. Adyen's 2018 to 2025 posts describe PostgreSQL clusters; its 2021 account says accounting was sharded round-robin, that rebalancing was not implemented, and that clusters exchange 'back and forth messages' to stay aligned, while templates guarantee that the records sum to zero. That is the documented difference: Stripe invested in moving data between shards and verifies its ledger after the fact (2024), Adyen in not needing to move it and in checking at write time (2021). That both rely on idempotent operations and later verification instead of a global transaction is an inference from these mechanisms; neither company states it, and which data is replicated synchronously, read consistency and the cross-cluster protocol are not public.

role.contribution: Shows how the record that chapter 37 says must be right stays right once it no longer fits in one database, and gives the reader the consistency boundary and the outbox as the small-scale version.

transition_in.carries_over: Chapter 37's split: the answering path is kept independent of the record, and the record may lag but may not be wrong.
transition_in.introduces: The consequence of that split: the record has to be kept right on its own terms, in databases that have themselves been divided into shards, without a transaction that covers all of them.

posts.title: Where the Data Lives: Multi-Region Operation and Data Residency
posts.question: What decides where a payment platform runs and where its data stays, and how much of Stripe's and Adyen's answer is public?

know: The difference between data residency (where data is stored) and data localization (a law that requires it), and what active-active and active-passive mean.
The Reserve Bank of India's 2018 storage rule and its 2019 clarification, and what Stripe's India page (updated 2023) says the move cost in features.

What is documented about hosting: Stripe on Amazon Web Services (2023, 2024, current documentation); Adyen on its own infrastructure in data centers (2021, 2025, 2026) with five integration regions named and its data centers listed by continent or country.

What is not public for either company: which AWS regions Stripe uses and how many, the cities of Adyen's data centers, and how one region or data center takes over from another (Adyen states only that its load balancers fail over between data centers).
believe: A localization law is a product constraint as much as a storage one: identifiers, saved cards and fraud signals stop crossing the border.
A statement about a provider's regions or failover that the provider has not published should be asked for in writing, not inferred.
can_do: Answer 'where is our customers' payment data' for each provider with what is documented, and list what must be asked of the provider.
Say what a new localization rule would change for stored cards, fraud checks and reporting in the affected country.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a confident sentence about a provider's regions, the reader separates the part the public record supports from the parts it does not.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A colleague writes in a design document: 'Stripe runs active-active in three AWS regions, so our European members' data never leaves the EU.' Which parts of this sentence does the public record support, as of November 2026?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Only that Stripe runs on AWS. No AWS region is named and no count given; Stripe states active-active nowhere; Stripe's data-processing documents describe transfer mechanisms for European personal data, and no EU-residency product statement was found. The sentence should be replaced by a question to the provider.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a new localization law in a country the chapter does not discuss, the reader names what changes for a merchant, going by the documented India case.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A country announces that payment data about transactions in the country must be stored only inside it. Going by what happened in India, name three things a merchant using a global provider there should expect to change.
acceptance_criteria.expected: Any three of: data for that country is stored on servers in the country and kept apart; saved payment details cannot be copied in or out; the same card gets a different fingerprint there than elsewhere, so duplicate and fraud checks stop matching across the border; some features (Stripe listed its card updater, revenue recognition in Billing and its Sigma reporting product) are disabled or changed; processing abroad may still be allowed with a deadline to bring the data back (24 hours in India's 2019 clarification).

acceptance_criteria.statement: The chapter contains no inferred topology: every Stripe and Adyen statement about hosting, regions or failover is a dated documented fact or the words 'not public', and a named section lists where the evidence stops.
The chapter is no longer than its evidence: it does not exceed about 3,800 words before Sources and Evidence.

thesis.question: What decides where a payment platform runs and where its data stays, and how much of Stripe's and Adyen's answer is public?
thesis.claim: Where a localization law applies, it settles where payment data is stored before any latency or availability goal, and elsewhere the provider's hosting model does.
