Stripe's 'total volume' is not defined in its annual letters, is unaudited, and changed name between letters; Adyen's processed volume comes from an audited report and includes volume it processes without acquiring; PayPal's total payment volume is net of reversals and excludes gateway-exclusive transactions; Square's gross payment volume is net of refunds and excludes buy-now-pay-later; Checkout.com's is a private company's press-release figure. Volume is not revenue: Adyen kept about 17 basis points of its 2025 volume as net revenue, and Stripe has never published revenue or margin, so 'earns the most' has no source.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The page that carries the part's closing sets the cases, the comparison and the changes in motion against the opening's two dated facts (Adyen's April 2026 sentence about acquired technologies and the bank in Stripe's US acquirer list), states what they have in common, and leads into the journal's closing on the same page; it does not only list trends and hand off to the reference pages.

thesis.question: What do the public records of Stripe and Adyen show about how the two came to build payment infrastructure differently, and how far does the reading 'Adyen owns the regulated money path, Stripe owns the developer's abstraction over it' hold?
thesis.claim: The records show an order of construction, not a division of territory, and they show sequence more than motive: Adyen, founded in 2006, built on an acquiring license it obtained in its first years and on enterprise customers, and became a bank (EU 2017, US 2021, UK 2023) on one platform it built and runs on servers it manages itself, while Stripe launched in 2011 with an API for developers and assembled the regulated layer afterward, market by market, from e-money licenses, named acquirers, most of them partner banks, and, since 2025, narrow charters. The reading holds for banking and hosting, fails for card acquiring in Europe and much of Asia-Pacific, where Stripe's own entities are the acquirer, cannot be tested on Stripe's motives or on how much volume each named acquirer carries, because Stripe has published neither, and by 2026 each company was moving toward the other's position.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the two made opposite and stable architectural choices: Adyen the bank that owns the whole chain, Stripe the software layer over other people's banks, so that choosing between them is choosing between owning the money path and renting it. Its commercial version is 'Stripe for startups, Adyen for enterprises'.
thesis.so_what: A team that accepts the claim stops choosing a provider by its slogan and compares bet by bet, with a date on every row: which entity acquires and holds funds in each country it sells in, what the pricing default is, which products were built and which bought, and what the provider has not published. It also treats the choice as one to revisit, as Larkfield (fictional) does with 44% of its volume on Stripe, 56% on Adyen and a rehearsed switch between them (K8).
thesis.how_why: Each company's own documents carry the argument. Adyen's 2025 annual report says it chose to 'develop and operate the essential layers of the financial stack ourselves' and to work 'without relying on partner banks'; Stripe's site says 'Stripe is not a bank' and its 2023 release says 'We couldn't run without AWS'. Those support the reading. Stripe's acquirer disclosure (accessed November 2026) names Stripe entities as acquirer across Europe and much of Asia-Pacific and lists a Stripe limited-purpose bank among its US acquirers (the Georgia regulator's bulletin dates its approval to 30 June 2025 and its start of business to 28 May 2026; the US regulator of national banks gave Stripe's Bridge preliminary conditional approval for a trust charter in February 2026); Adyen reports 84% of 2025 volume as full-stack and names banking partners in locations where it has no acquiring license; on 1 July 2026 Adyen closed two acquisitions, the only ones its history page lists, one of which it described in June 2026 as run under an incubator model. Those cut against it. Stripe has published no reason for using partner banks, no share of volume per acquirer and no revenue; Adyen lists the countries and regions where it has an acquiring connection, names its acquiring entity for some markets and gives no complete list per country; it says the integration of what it bought has begun and gives no date for its completion. On those points the part says the record is silent and does not infer.

supporting_claims.claim: Stripe's dated record shows a company that made the developer's interface its product first (one API and object model, self-serve onboarding, a published history of its own API design) and then widened from it in two directions: outward into a suite of billing, tax and finance products, several of them bought, and downward into the regulated layer, which it holds as a non-bank through e-money licenses, partner banks and, since 2025, narrow charters. Its public numbers are volume and customer counts it selects, never revenue.

Adyen's dated record shows a company that chose to operate the regulated layers itself for enterprise customers (its own platform, acquiring, banking licenses and data-center capacity) and reports the result in audited figures; the single platform has edges Adyen itself discloses, and since 1 July 2026 it describes Adyen's payments and banking, not the whole company, because loyalty and usage billing were bought.

Compared bet by bet, the documented differences are of three kinds: differences of kind that hold in November 2026 (a bank against an e-money institution with partner banks; own data-center capacity against AWS), differences of default, sequence or degree that narrowed in 2025 and 2026 (acquiring, build or buy, first customers and pricing, billing products, the API model), and questions the public record cannot decide; a customer should therefore choose per bet and per country, not per brand.

PayPal, Checkout.com and Block show that the two anchors are not the ends of one line: each holds something neither anchor does (a consumer wallet, a set of acquiring licenses started later, the seller's till and an industrial bank), and read together they support the inference, labeled as the author's, that what a provider holds traces to the customer relationship it started with.

The changes under way in November 2026 (agent-initiated payments, stablecoins, instant account-to-account payments, new EU rules) move or shorten a promise in the payment chain without removing the need to track it, and each company's response repeats its starting point while the two keep converging: Stripe co-authors protocols and owns a stablecoin stack, Adyen implements several protocols and has published one clause on stablecoins, and both bought a usage-billing company in 2026.

role.contribution: Tests the second half of the journal thesis against the two companies' own dated records: without this part the book's 'Where They Differ' tables would remain separate observations, one table per chapter, and the claim about which side of the gap each company owns would be asserted but never checked. It also carries the journal's closing.

additional_patterns.applies_to: case-stripe and case-adyen: the same questions, in the same order, put to each company
payments-what-is-moving: from positions as they stood to changes dated 2025 and 2026

flow.rationale: The part intro states the reading to be tested and the rules of evidence; the two cases give each company's record on its own terms; the comparison reasons across them; the contrast cases test that reasoning on three companies that started elsewhere; the last chapter shows the positions moving and closes the book. Putting the comparison before the cases would ask the reader to accept a map whose rows have no dated record behind them, which is how the 'startups versus enterprises' cliché is made. Putting the contrast cases before the comparison would leave nothing to contrast with. Stripe comes before Adyen because the reader, an engineer, has most likely met Stripe's API already, so Adyen can be read against something known. The chapter on what is moving must be last: it needs both positions to say what is changing, and it carries the journal's closing.

hook.content: On 9 April 2026 an Adyen press release said: 'Unlike many providers that rely on a patchwork of acquired technologies and third-party integrations, Adyen has built its entire financial technology stack on a single platform.' Fourteen days later Adyen announced that it would buy Talon.One for €750 million, and on 11 June that it would buy Orb for $335 million; both deals closed on 1 July. By November 2026 the page on which Stripe, whose site says 'Stripe is not a bank', lists its US acquirers named, next to five partner banks, 'Stripe MALPB, 505 N Angier Avenue NE, Atlanta': a limited-purpose bank of Stripe's own.

opening.bridge: From the reader's own shorthand for the two companies (the bank and the API, the enterprise one and the startup one), which the eight parts' 'Where They Differ' tables have so far neither confirmed nor refuted, to the companies' own documents read with dates: what each said it chose, what its filings and legal pages show, and where neither says anything. Larkfield, the fictional platform this book follows, runs on both, so the question is practical: what exactly differs between the 44% of its volume on Stripe and the 56% on Adyen.
opening.roadmap: How the cases are read (documented, widely reported, inferred, not public; every claim dated; Stripe is private and Adyen is listed, so their numbers are not alike). Then Stripe as a case; Adyen as a case; the bets compared one by one; three other answers (PayPal and Braintree, Checkout.com, Block); and what is moving in November 2026, which also closes the book.

closing.synthesis: Read together, the two cases, the comparison, the three contrasts and the changes of 2026 say something none says alone: what looks like a provider's architecture is the trace of where it started, whom it served first and which permission it could get, and that trace keeps being redrawn. Stripe added banks under its API; Adyen added bought software beside its platform; the newest changes are being absorbed the same way, each from its own side. What did not move in any of the records is the work the rest of the book describes: knowing who promised what, and proving that the records agree.
closing.so_what: A provider choice is a dated decision about specific promises (who acquires, who holds the funds, who answers for a loss, whose records you reconcile against), to be written down with its evidence and reviewed, not an identity to adopt. A reader who works this way can add, change or combine providers without redesigning the payment system around a slogan.
closing.callback: The opening's two facts from 2026: Adyen's sentence about 'a patchwork of acquired technologies', overtaken by two acquisitions within three months, and the bank in the acquirer list of the company that 'is not a bank'. Both slogans were out of date inside a year; the integrations built on them last longer.

takeaway.content: Fill in the provider comparison card from the toolkit for each provider you use or are evaluating: per country, the entity that acquires and the one that holds funds; the pricing default; the hosting dependency; for each product, whether it was built or bought and when; and, for every row, the date, the source and what is not public. Keep the provider exit plan card beside it.

transition_in.carries_over: The four journeys of Part IX followed one payment across every mechanism on both providers and showed the same payment recorded in two vocabularies: a retrievable object on Stripe and a reference plus events on Adyen, funds made available per transaction on one and per sales day on the other. With the 'Where They Differ' tables of Parts I to VIII, the reader now holds a table of documented differences from every chapter and no account of where they come from.
transition_in.introduces: The companies themselves as the unit of analysis: their dated histories, licenses, figures and stated strategies, and the test of whether one explanation (which side of the gap each chose to own) accounts for the differences the reader has seen.

How the evidence is read: company documents researched on 17 November 2026; every claim dated; documented, widely reported and inferred statements kept apart; Stripe is private and publishes volume and customer counts in annual letters, Adyen is listed and files audited accounts, so their figures are not alike; each case ends with what the record could not establish.

The reading under test: that Adyen chose to own the regulated money path and Stripe the developer's abstraction over it, and that the part finds this supported for some choices, contradicted for one and undecidable for others.

posts.title: Case: Stripe, the Developer Platform That Became Financial Infrastructure
posts.question: What does Stripe's dated public record show about how a developer platform became financial infrastructure, and which of its practices can a builder use?

know: The history in dated steps: launch in 2011, Connect in October 2012, Billing, Issuing and Terminal in 2018, Tax and Revenue Recognition in 2021; acquisitions separated into announced and completed (TaxJar and Recko 2021, Lemon Squeezy 2024, Bridge completed February 2025, Metronome completed January 2026, OpenRouter and Parafin announced and not confirmed closed on 17 November 2026); the self-description moving from 'economic infrastructure for the internet' to 'the programmable financial services company'.

The regulated layer as Stripe documents it: e-money institutions in the UK (2017 page) and Ireland (2019), state money-transmitter licenses in the US, 'Stripe is not a bank', and an acquirer disclosure (accessed November 2026) that names Stripe entities as acquirer in the EEA, the UK and much of Asia-Pacific, other named acquirers, most of them banks, in markets that include the United States, Canada, Japan, India and Thailand, and a Stripe limited-purpose bank, in business since 28 May 2026, among the six US acquirers.

The published figures with what they are: 'total volume' of $1.9 trillion in 2025, undefined and renamed between letters; 'more than 5 million businesses directly or via platforms'; a Revenue suite 'on track' for a $1 billion run rate; 'robustly profitable' with no measure named; no revenue, margin or headcount since November 2022; valuations that are prices from funding rounds and tender offers.

The documented engineering record and its age: API versioning and idempotency (2017), the payments API's first ten years (2020), the Ledger (2024, 2026), reliability figures from the 2023 letter, hosting on AWS (2023), and where it stops (sponsor-bank shares, the internals behind the newer products, which regions it runs in).
believe: Stripe is not a thin layer over other people's banks in every market, and not a bank in any; which it is depends on the country and the product.
What a builder can take from Stripe is its interface discipline, which is documented and works at any size, not its scale machinery or its product count.
can_do: Say, for a given country, who Stripe names as the acquirer and what kind of regulated entity stands behind a Stripe balance, and what Stripe does not publish about either.
Read a Stripe figure and state what it measures, who selected it and what it cannot be compared with.
Separate, in Stripe's engineering publications, practices to adopt from machinery sized for Stripe, with the age of each source.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given the claim that Stripe does not touch the money, the reader answers from Stripe's own legal pages, by region, and says what remains unpublished.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A colleague says: 'Stripe is software on top of banks; it never acquires a payment or holds funds itself.' Using only this chapter: what does Stripe's own record show, region by region, and what does it leave unsaid?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Stripe's acquirer disclosure names a Stripe entity as the acquirer (the network member that submits the merchant's card transactions and receives the money for them) in the EEA, the UK and much of Asia-Pacific; those entities are e-money institutions regulated in Ireland and the UK, which may hold customer funds as safeguarded balances but are not banks. In the United States, Canada, Japan, India and Thailand Stripe is a payment facilitator or aggregator under named acquirers, most of them banks (card companies in Japan), and the US list now also has Stripe's own Georgia limited-purpose bank, in business since 28 May 2026. 'Stripe is not a bank': deposit accounts in its treasury product are provided by a partner bank. A direct technical connection to a card network, which Stripe announced for six networks in 2020, is not the same as being the acquirer of record. Not public: the share of volume per acquirer, which merchants the Georgia bank acquires for and how much it processes, the names of the safeguarding banks, and Stripe's reasons for the partner-bank model.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a sentence that misuses Stripe's published numbers, the reader corrects each figure from the chapter.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An investment memo says: 'Stripe's revenue grew 34% to $1.9 trillion in 2025, it employs about 7,000 people, and its market capitalization is $159 billion.' Using only this chapter: correct the sentence.
acceptance_criteria.expected: $1.9 trillion is 'total volume' generated by businesses running on Stripe, up 34%: the value of payments moved, of which a provider keeps a small fraction, not revenue; the letters do not define it and the metric's name changed between years. Stripe has never published revenue or margin; its letters say 'profitable' without naming a measure. 'Almost 7,000' is from a company email of November 2022, the last official headcount. $159 billion is the price of a February 2026 tender offer for employees' shares, not a market capitalization; Stripe is private.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader separates the Stripe practices a small payments team should adopt from the machinery it should not copy, with the reason and the age of the evidence.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A payments team of twelve at a travel-booking company wants to 'build like Stripe' and proposes sharding its database and deploying hundreds of times a day. Using only this chapter: what should the team take from Stripe's record, what should it leave, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Take: an idempotency key on every money-moving request; dated API versions that a client pins and upgrades on a schedule; a payment object with explicit states that a client can read again after a timeout; an immutable double-entry ledger whose clearing accounts must return to zero, checked continuously. Leave: the database platform and its shards, a test fleet of about 1.4 million tests, about 400 deploys a day of one core service, rollouts inspected against tens of thousands of metrics. Reason: the first group is about correctness at the interface and holds at any volume; the second answers Stripe's volume and engineer count. Several of the sources are from 2017 to 2020 and may describe replaced systems; the chapter says which later documents confirm them.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter establish about Stripe, in what order, and from what kinds of source?
acceptance_criteria.expected: How to read the case and where sources were unreachable; history and acquisitions by date; the interface as the first product; the suite; licenses, partner banks and charters; the figures and what they are; the documented engineering record; what transfers and what does not; where the evidence stops. Sources: annual letters, press releases, legal and documentation pages, engineering posts, each dated, with trade press named as such.

thesis.question: What does Stripe's dated public record show about how a developer platform became financial infrastructure, and which of its practices can a builder use?
thesis.claim: Stripe's record shows a company that made the developer's interface its first product and then widened from it in two directions: outward into a suite of billing, tax and finance products, several of them bought, and downward into the regulated layer, which it holds as a non-bank assembled per market from e-money licenses, named acquirers, most of them partner banks, and, since 2025, narrow charters. A builder can use the interface discipline Stripe has documented (idempotency keys, dated versions, a payment object whose state can be read again, a ledger whose clearing accounts must empty) and should not copy its sharded data platform, its deploy rate or its product count.
thesis.disputed_by: Two opposite views, each held by experienced engineers: that Stripe is a thin software layer over other companies' banks and acquirers, suited to startups, and so has little to teach about the money path; and that Stripe is the model architecture, so that a serious payments team should reproduce its sharded data platform, its deploy rate and its breadth.
thesis.so_what: A team evaluating Stripe asks which entity acquires and which holds funds in each country it sells in, treats the named acquirer as data that can change, and tests the integration between Stripe products that arrived by acquisition instead of assuming it. A team building its own payment service takes the four interface practices into its design and budgets nothing for imitating Stripe's infrastructure.
thesis.how_why: Stripe's 2022 letter lists 'simple, reliable, secure, and developer-friendly APIs' among the ways it pursues its mission, and its engineering posts (2017, 2020) describe the API as something designed, versioned and corrected over years: idempotency keys and dated versions in 2017 posts, the payment object and its states in 2020, and the Ledger with clearing accounts that return to zero in 2024. Those four practices concern correctness at the interface and work at any volume; the data platform and the deploy rate answer Stripe's volume and engineer count, which a builder does not have. The products around it came in dated steps and partly by purchase: tax (TaxJar, 2021), reconciliation (Recko, 2021), stablecoins (Bridge, 2025), usage billing (Metronome, 2026). The regulated layer is visible in legal pages, not in strategy statements: Stripe entities, regulated as e-money institutions in Ireland and the UK, are the named acquirer in the EEA, the UK and much of Asia-Pacific; other acquirers, most of them banks, are named for markets that include North America, Japan, India and Thailand; a Georgia limited-purpose bank of Stripe's own appears in the US list (the state regulator's bulletin dates its approval to 30 June 2025 and its start of business to 28 May 2026), and a February 2026 letter from the US regulator of national banks gives Bridge preliminary conditional approval for a trust charter. Stripe has not said why it uses partner banks, what share each acquirer carries, or what it earns: it publishes volume ($1.9 trillion in 2025, undefined) and customer counts, never revenue. The chapter stops where those documents stop.

role.contribution: Supplies the first company's record on its own terms, including the facts that do not fit the 'abstraction only' reading, so that the comparison in chapter 48 rests on dated documents and not on Stripe's reputation.

transition_in.carries_over: The part intro's reading under test (Adyen the regulated money path, Stripe the developer's abstraction), its two dated facts from 2026 and its rules for labeling evidence.
transition_in.introduces: The first of the two records in full: Stripe's history, products, licenses, figures and engineering publications by date, read for what supports the label 'the abstraction' and what does not.

posts.title: Case: Adyen, the Single Platform With a Banking Licence
posts.question: What does Adyen's dated public record show about building payments as one platform under its own banking license, and which of its practices can a builder use?

know: The history in dated steps: founded in Amsterdam in 2006; a European acquiring license, which its history page dates only to the period 2006 to 2012; banking license 2017; listing on Euronext Amsterdam in June 2018; US federal branch 2021; embedded financial products March 2022; UK banking authorization September 2023; the 2023 margin fall (55% in 2022 to 46% in 2023) and recovery (50% in 2024, 53% in 2025); Talon.One and Orb announced in April and June 2026 and closed on 1 July 2026.

The single-platform bet in Adyen's own words (2025 annual report): operate 'the essential layers of the financial stack ourselves', 'a single platform built entirely in-house', licenses held to work 'without relying on partner banks', with data centers as the main capital expenditure (5% of net revenue in 2025, 7% expected for 2026).

The figures with their definitions: processed volume, net revenue (what Adyen keeps after passing on interchange and scheme fees), EBITDA margin, take rate (17.0 basis points in 2025), full-stack share (84%), in-person volume (€310.9 billion, 22% of volume), the three pillars (Digital, Unified Commerce, Platforms), top ten merchants at 11% of revenue.

Where the single platform stops by Adyen's own disclosures (16% of volume not full-stack, banking partners named as a concentration risk in locations where it has no acquiring license, Orb described in June 2026 as run as an 'incubator' that keeps serving other providers, 'convergence' stated as intent with no date) and where the public record stops (the cities, operators and number of its data centers beyond six named regions, the identity of the single large-volume customer, what has been integrated of the acquired products).
believe: 'Single platform, built in-house' is a dated description of Adyen's payments and banking core, accurate there, and no longer a description of the whole company.

Owning the regulated layer is a choice with a visible price (capital, supervision, capital expenditure) and a visible return in Adyen's accounts; it is not available to, or sensible for, most builders.
can_do: State which Adyen products run on the platform it built and which were bought in 2026, and what Adyen has and has not said about integrating them.
Read Adyen's volume, net revenue, margin and take rate together and explain a year in which they move in different directions.
Name the practices in Adyen's record that a builder can adopt and the assets it cannot.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given the claim that everything bought from Adyen is one platform, the reader answers as of November 2026 with the dated facts and the stated limits.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An architect at a retailer says in November 2026: 'Adyen builds everything itself on one platform, so whatever we buy from them is one integration with one set of reports.' Using only this chapter: is that right?
acceptance_criteria.expected: For payments, acquiring, terminals and the banking products it is what Adyen states: 'a single platform built entirely in-house' on its own licenses (annual report 2025). It is no longer true of everything Adyen sells: on 1 July 2026 Adyen closed the purchases of Talon.One (loyalty and promotions, €750 million) and Orb (usage billing, $335 million). Adyen says Talon.One's engine is being integrated into its architecture; in June 2026 it said that Orb runs under 'an incubator model', keeps 'supporting multi-PSP environments', and that 'the strategic intent is convergence', with no date; on 28 October 2026 it wrote of 'the successful ongoing integration of Talon.One and Orb' without saying what has been joined. Until then a customer using those products should expect separate systems and ask Adyen what is shared. No Adyen document says it has abandoned building in-house; a 9 April 2026 release still contrasted Adyen with providers that rely on 'acquired technologies'.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given Adyen's 2025 figures moving in different directions, the reader explains them from the definitions and from what Adyen reports.
acceptance_criteria.probe: In 2025 Adyen's processed volume grew 8% and its net revenue grew 18%. A colleague concludes that Adyen raised its prices. Using only this chapter: what does Adyen's own reporting say?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Processed volume grew 8% as reported and 21% excluding a single large-volume customer that Adyen does not name; net revenue, which is what Adyen keeps after passing on interchange and scheme fees, grew 18%. The take rate (net revenue divided by processed volume) rose from 15.5 to 17.0 basis points, which Adyen attributes to 'changes in the overall merchant mix', not to price increases. Adyen prices in volume tiers, so less volume from a very large customer lowers volume more than revenue. In the first half of 2026 the take rate was 16.2 basis points, which Adyen attributes to 'expected volume tiering'.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader separates what a builder can adopt from Adyen's record from the assets that cannot be copied, and names the limit Adyen itself discloses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A logistics platform with a payments team of nine reads this chapter and wants 'what Adyen has'. Using only this chapter: what can it adopt, what can it not, and what does Adyen say about how its own largest customers buy?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Adopt: one accounting core for every money movement with entries that must sum to zero, checked when written (Adyen's 2021 account, five years old); one place where each improvement takes effect for all customers; API versions visible in every request. Cannot copy: banking licenses in three jurisdictions, data-center capacity bought with 5 to 7% of net revenue, an estate of 878,000 transacting terminals. Adyen's own risk section says large enterprise merchants typically work with several payment providers and may shift volume, so even its customers do not treat one platform as the only one.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter establish about Adyen, in what order, and from what kinds of source?
acceptance_criteria.expected: How to read the case; history by date; the single-platform bet in Adyen's words; licenses and what they allow; unified commerce and terminals; platforms and financial products; the 2026 acquisitions and what they change; figures with definitions; the documented engineering record and its age; what transfers; where the evidence stops. Sources: the audited annual report, shareholder letters and business updates, press releases, license and documentation pages, engineering posts, each dated.

thesis.question: What does Adyen's dated public record show about building payments as one platform under its own banking license, and which of its practices can a builder use?
thesis.claim: Adyen's record shows a company that chose to operate the regulated layers itself for enterprise customers (one platform built in-house, its own acquiring and banking licenses in the EU, the US and the UK, its own data-center capacity) and that reports its volume, net revenue and margin in audited figures; Adyen itself discloses where the single platform stops (16% of 2025 volume was not full-stack, and it names banking partners in locations where it has no acquiring license), and since 1 July 2026 the phrase describes Adyen's payments and banking core and not the whole company, because loyalty and usage billing were bought and Adyen describes one of them, Orb, as run under 'an incubator model'. A builder can adopt the practice of one accounting core and one place for every change; the licenses, the data centers and the terminal estate are assets built over two decades, not a design a builder can adopt.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that Adyen proves building everything in-house on one platform is the correct architecture for payments, that the company still builds and does not buy, and that the 2026 acquisitions are a footnote; or the opposite view, that the acquisitions show the single platform was always a slogan.
thesis.so_what: A customer integrating Adyen before July 2026 touched one platform; one that adds Orb or Talon.One should ask what is shared (credentials, events, reports) and plan for separate systems until Adyen says otherwise. A builder notes that Adyen attributes its 53% margin to the single platform, that the attribution is Adyen's own, and that the platform and licenses behind it took from 2006 to 2023 to assemble; the margin is not evidence for a design a team could reproduce in a year.
thesis.how_why: The annual report for 2025 states the choice as a sequence: first 'our single global platform', so that an improvement 'takes effect everywhere, without reintegration work'; then 'our own banking licenses in the EU, US, and UK', to work 'without relying on partner banks'; data centers are the main capital expenditure. Adyen credits the platform for its margin ('the underlying operational efficiency inherent to our single-platform architecture', H1 2026), which is its own attribution, not an independent finding. The same documents mark the edges: 84% of 2025 volume was full-stack; concentration risk sits 'at banking partners in locations where there are no own direct acquiring licenses'; Orb is preserved under 'an incubator model' and keeps 'supporting multi-PSP environments'. In August 2026 Adyen wrote 'we are no longer just a payments company'. Its 2021 engineering account describes one accounting framework whose entries must sum to zero when written, which is the practice a builder can take. Its posts on the platform's architecture are mostly from 2018 to 2021, with later ones on partitioning (2023 to 2025) and one of 2026 that adds scale, so the chapter's account of internals is short and dated; the cities and operators of its data centers (it names six regions), what has been integrated of the acquisitions and the identity of the single large-volume customer behind its 2025 volume figures are not public.

role.contribution: Supplies the second company's record, including Adyen's own statements of where its platform and licenses stop and the 2026 acquisitions, so that the comparison does not set Stripe's documents against Adyen's slogan.

transition_in.carries_over: Stripe's order of construction from chapter 46: the interface first, then products around it, then the regulated layer assembled per market as a non-bank, with volume and customer counts as its only public numbers.
transition_in.introduces: A company that built in the other order (the acquiring license and the platform first, the bank next, adjacent software last and by purchase) and that reports audited figures, so the same questions get differently shaped answers.

posts.title: Two Ways to Build It: The Architectural Bets Compared
posts.question: On which architectural bets do Stripe and Adyen demonstrably differ in November 2026, and what should a customer choosing or combining them do with each difference?

know: The map of bets, each with a dated fact for both companies or the words 'not public': license and money-holding (a credit institution with branches against e-money institutions, state licenses, partner banks and, in business since 28 May 2026, a Georgia limited-purpose acquiring bank of Stripe's own); acquiring (84% full-stack, with 14 countries and regions listed as having an Adyen acquiring connection, against own entities in Europe and much of Asia-Pacific and other named acquirers, most of them banks, elsewhere); build or buy (two acquisitions, both in 2026, against at least ten since 2020); one platform or a suite; first customers and default pricing (Interchange++ with tiers against a published blended rate, with interchange-plus listed among Stripe's custom options); hosting (data centers whose servers Adyen manages itself, with six regions named and no cities or operators, against AWS by Stripe's 2023 statement, with no AWS region named); billing and revenue products (no billing product and no first-party tax engine of Adyen's own found until Orb, and Adyen's statement that it is not a merchant of record, against Billing since 2018, plus tax, revenue recognition and a merchant-of-record product for digital goods); platforms.

Which of these are differences of kind, which of default, sequence or degree, and which the public record cannot decide: Stripe's reasons for partner banks, the volume share of each acquirer, the acquiring entity per country at Adyen, realized prices, any independent measure of approval rates.

Why 'one platform against a suite' compares two different things: a statement about Adyen's engineering and operations with a statement about Stripe's packaging; Stripe has published nothing about a single code base.

The integrator-visible consequences the earlier parts documented: a payment a client can read again against a reference plus events; idempotency keys kept at least 24 hours against 7 to 14 days; a version set per account or header against one written in every URL; published rate limits against none published for payments; funds made available per transaction against a pre-financed sales-day payout.
believe: The choice between the two is made bet by bet and country by country; neither 'the bank against the API' nor 'enterprises against startups' survives the dated record.
A stated reason for a difference is an inference unless the company gave it, and should be labeled so.
can_do: For a described business, list which documented differences bear on its decision, which do not, and what it must ask each provider because the record is silent.
Classify any claimed Stripe and Adyen difference as one of kind, one of degree or default, or one that cannot be decided from public sources, with a dated fact for each side.
Fill in the provider comparison card for a business that runs both.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given two businesses the chapter does not describe, the reader says which documented differences matter to each and avoids deciding by company size alone.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Two companies ask the same question. A: thirty engineers, sells software subscriptions online in twenty countries, bills partly by usage, has no finance team that audits card costs. B: a retailer with four hundred stores in eight European countries, billing done in its ERP, a treasury team that reconciles cost by card type. Using only this chapter: for each, which documented differences between Stripe and Adyen bear on the choice, which do not, and what can neither record tell them?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A: Stripe's own subscription engine (since 2018), usage metering and Metronome, tax and revenue-recognition products, a published blended rate, self-serve activation and a payment object it can read again all bear on the choice; Adyen had no billing product of its own until it bought Orb in July 2026, which it described in June 2026 as run under an incubator model and says it is integrating. The bank-or-not difference matters little to A. B: Adyen's reported in-person volume (€310.9 billion in 2025, 22% of its volume) and terminal estate, Interchange++ pricing with volume tiers as the default, acquiring across the EEA under one banking license, and a sales-day payout that Adyen pre-finances bear on the choice; the billing difference does not. Stripe offers in-person payments and interchange-plus pricing on request but publishes no in-person volume. Neither record gives realized prices, an independent measure of approval rates, or volume per acquirer; both companies must be asked. Size alone decides nothing: each now sells to the other's first customers.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a list of claimed differences, the reader classifies each as of kind, of degree or default, or undecidable, with one dated fact per company.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter, classify each statement as a difference of kind that holds in November 2026, a difference of degree or default, or not decidable from the public record, and give one dated fact for each company: (1) 'Adyen is a bank and Stripe is not.' (2) 'Adyen acquires itself and Stripe uses sponsors.' (3) 'Adyen builds and Stripe buys.' (4) 'Adyen runs its own data centers and Stripe runs on a public cloud.' (5) 'Stripe chose partner banks to enter markets faster.'
acceptance_criteria.expected: (1) Kind: Adyen N.V. is a credit institution licensed in 2017, with a US branch (2021) and UK authorization (2023); Stripe states 'Stripe is not a bank' (2026) and operates e-money institutions and state money-transmitter licenses. (2) Degree: Adyen reports 84% full-stack volume (2025), lists 14 countries and regions with an Adyen acquiring connection (n.d., accessed 2026) and names banking partners where it has no license; Stripe's disclosure (accessed 2026) names its own entities as acquirer in Europe and much of Asia-Pacific, other named acquirers, most of them banks, in North America and some Asian markets, and its own Georgia bank, in business since 28 May 2026, in the US. (3) Degree since 2026: Adyen closed two acquisitions on 1 July 2026, the only ones its history page lists; Stripe has named at least ten since 2020. (4) Kind: Adyen says most of its capital expenditure is data centers (2025) and names six data-center regions; Stripe said 'We couldn't run without AWS' (2023). (5) Not decidable: Stripe has published no reason; the statement is an inference and the chapter labels it so.

acceptance_criteria.statement: In the comparison map, every Stripe cell and every Adyen cell is a documented fact with its year or the words 'Not public', and every reason offered for a difference is introduced as inference.
A reader of the introduction alone can predict the bets the chapter compares, in order, and how it sorts them.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: which bets will this chapter compare, in what order, and into what kinds will it sort the differences?
acceptance_criteria.expected: License and money-holding; acquiring and connectivity; build or buy; one platform or a suite; first customers, the API model and pricing; hosting; billing and revenue products; platforms. Sorted into differences of kind that still hold, differences of degree or default that narrowed in 2025 and 2026, and questions the public record cannot decide, each with what it means for a customer.

thesis.question: On which architectural bets do Stripe and Adyen demonstrably differ in November 2026, and what should a customer choosing or combining them do with each difference?
thesis.claim: Two of the bets are differences of kind that both records document: who holds the money (a licensed bank against e-money institutions with partner banks) and who runs the machines (own data-center capacity against AWS). The rest (acquiring, build or buy, first customers and pricing, billing products, the API model) are differences of default, sequence or degree that narrowed in 2025 and 2026, and 'one platform against a suite' sets an engineering statement beside a packaging statement. A customer should therefore treat the two kinds differently: for a difference of kind, establish per country which entity will hold its funds and what it depends on; for a difference of degree or default, compare the default it will live with and ask for the alternative; and decide on neither company's slogan.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that the two companies embody opposite architectures that follow from their customers, 'Stripe for startups, Adyen for enterprises', so that company size settles the choice; and the engineer's version of it, that Adyen owns the stack and Stripe rents it, so that the comparison is one row long.
thesis.so_what: The decision becomes a card with rows and dates instead of a preference. A business that runs both, as Larkfield (fictional) does, knows which differences it must absorb in its own payment service (two fee models, two payout timings, two sets of regulated entities, two webhook contracts) and which it can ignore; a business choosing one knows which questions to put to the sales team because the public record does not answer them.
thesis.how_why: The 'Where They Differ' tables of Parts I to VIII, gathered, sort themselves by evidence. Where both companies have documented a structural fact, the difference is of kind: Adyen's banking licenses and Stripe's 'not a bank'; Adyen's data-center capital expenditure and Stripe's statement on AWS (2023; a 2024 AWS post co-written by Stripe engineers is consistent with it). Where the facts are the same in type and differ in amount, order or default, it is of degree: Stripe's own entities acquire in Europe and much of Asia-Pacific while Adyen is full-stack for 84% of volume; Stripe built Billing in 2018 and bought Metronome in 2026 while Adyen bought Orb in 2026; Stripe's default is a published blended rate with interchange-plus among its custom options, while Adyen's default is Interchange++ with volume tiers; each began with one kind of customer and now sells to the other's. Where one company has published nothing (Stripe's reasons for partner banks, its sponsor shares, its code structure; Adyen's integration dates and a complete list of its acquiring entities per country; either one's realized prices), the chapter says 'not public' and gives any reason only as labeled inference. The clearest integrator-facing differences are defaults. That they fit each company's first customers is the author's inference, and it is a statement about where the defaults came from, not about which customer should choose which company today: a self-serve, re-readable API with published limits on one side; one with methods and features enabled on request, explicit versions, longer retry windows and pre-financed payouts on the other.

role.contribution: Turns the two cases and the book's 'Where They Differ' tables into one argued map, and is the page on which the journal's provisional reading of the two companies is confirmed in part and corrected in part.

transition_in.carries_over: The two records as chapters 46 and 47 left them: Stripe, the interface first and the regulated layer assembled afterward as a non-bank; Adyen, the license and platform first and adjacent software bought in 2026; each with its own list of what is not public.
transition_in.introduces: The two set side by side on the same rows, with the 'Where They Differ' tables of Parts I to VIII gathered under them, a sorting of the differences by the kind of evidence behind each, and what a customer does with each row.

posts.title: Other Answers: PayPal and Braintree, Checkout.com, Block
posts.question: What do PayPal and Braintree, Checkout.com and Block each show about the Stripe and Adyen bets that the two companies alone cannot?

know: PayPal's FY2025 Form 10-K: 'a global, two-sided network' with 439 million active accounts; total payment volume of $1.79 trillion, defined net of reversals and excluding gateway-exclusive transactions; lower Braintree volume and revenue in the first half of 2025 after 'a stronger focus on profitable growth'; Braintree products 'generally have higher expense rates than other products and services'.

Checkout.com's 2026 releases (a private company's own figures): over $300 billion processed in 2025; $750 million of annualized net revenue; ten acquiring licenses in 56 countries; direct acquiring in the United States under a Georgia limited-purpose bank charter, announced on 9 September 2026 (the Georgia regulator dates the bank's start of business to 16 July 2026).

Block's FY2025 Form 10-K: more than 4.5 million sellers and $250 billion of Square gross payment volume, defined net of refunds; custom-designed hardware and seller software sold with payments; Square Financial Services, a Utah-chartered industrial loan company, operational since 1 March 2021.

Where the evidence stops: these are filings and press releases about business models; no first-party architecture evidence for PayPal, Braintree or Checkout.com was read, so the chapter makes no claim about how they are built.
believe: What a payment provider owns follows from the customer relationship it started with, and Stripe and Adyen are two of several such starting points, not the two ends of one line.
Volume figures from different companies cannot be ranked without their definitions.
can_do: Say which contrast case clarifies a given choice (a consumer wallet as an asset, an enterprise acquirer started later, seller software and hardware first) and what it implies about Stripe's and Adyen's positions.
Read a 10-K sentence about a processing business and say what it shows about the economics of unbranded card processing.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a claim that infers a processor's strength from its parent's volume, the reader corrects it from the filing's definitions and its statements about Braintree.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A marketplace founder says: 'PayPal processed $1.79 trillion in 2025, almost as much as Stripe, so Braintree is the safest home for our card processing.' Using only this chapter: what does PayPal's own filing say that bears on this?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The $1.79 trillion is PayPal's total payment volume across its branded wallet (PayPal, Venmo) and its unbranded processing, net of reversals and excluding gateway-exclusive transactions; it is not Braintree's volume and is not defined like Stripe's 'total volume'. The filing says volume and transaction revenue from Braintree fell in the first half of 2025 after 'a stronger focus on profitable growth and ongoing negotiations with merchants', and that Braintree products generally have higher expense rates than PayPal's other products. The asset the filing describes is the two-sided network of 439 million active accounts; unbranded processing (handling a merchant's own card form, which is what Stripe and Adyen sell) is the part with the higher expense rate. The chapter gives no evidence about Braintree's architecture or reliability.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given three unlike businesses, the reader matches each to the contrast case that clarifies its choice and says what the case implies about Stripe or Adyen.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: which of the three contrast cases should each of these read first, and what does it tell them about Stripe or Adyen? (a) A food-truck franchise choosing a till and card reader for 300 owner-operators. (b) An airline that wants a second acquirer beside Adyen. (c) A product team that asks why Stripe keeps promoting its Link wallet.
acceptance_criteria.expected: (a) Block: its customer is the seller buying an integrated till, with custom hardware and software and payments included; it serves millions of sellers where Adyen serves enterprises directly, and neither Adyen's terminal estate nor Stripe's developer-facing Terminal is that product. (b) Checkout.com: the enterprise proposition started later, with its own acquiring licenses and, since 2026 (in business from 16 July, announced on 9 September), direct US acquiring under a Georgia charter, the same narrow charter Stripe obtained; Adyen's own risk section expects large merchants to use several providers. (c) PayPal: the filing shows the consumer network is the asset and unbranded processing the part with the higher expense rate; Link (which Stripe says had over 250 million users in April 2026 and over 300 million in September 2026, undefined) is Stripe building the consumer side that a processor lacks, which is the chapter's inference, labeled as such; Adyen has no consumer wallet.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone can predict the three cases, the one choice each is used for and the limits of the evidence.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: which companies does this chapter cover, what single point is each used for, and what kind of evidence does it not have?
acceptance_criteria.expected: PayPal and Braintree for the two-sided consumer wallet as an asset beside a processor; Checkout.com for an enterprise acquirer built later with its own licenses; Block for seller software and hardware first with payments included. Evidence is 10-K filings and company releases with each figure's definition; there is no first-party evidence on how these companies' systems are built, and the chapter is short by design.

thesis.question: What do PayPal and Braintree, Checkout.com and Block each show about the Stripe and Adyen bets that the two companies alone cannot?
thesis.claim: Each contrast adds one case the pair lacks: PayPal's filing describes a two-sided network of 439 million accounts beside an unbranded processing business that it says carries higher expense rates; Checkout.com sells to enterprises with its own acquiring licenses, as Adyen does, and in 2026 began acquiring in the United States under the same narrow charter that Stripe obtained; Block began with the seller's till and holds a third kind of bank, a Utah industrial loan company. Read together they support an inference that is the author's and not the companies': the regulated permissions and assets a provider holds are the ones its first customer relationship required, and a provider whose first license had nothing to do with its first customers would count against it.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that payment providers sit on one spectrum from developer-first to enterprise-first, with Stripe and Adyen at its ends and every other company somewhere between them, so that the contrast cases add scale comparisons and nothing else.
thesis.so_what: A reader comparing providers adds a row the Stripe and Adyen comparison lacks: who owns the relationship with the payer and with the seller, because that relationship determines which data the provider sees and, on the author's reading, which products it adds. It also explains moves that the two-company view makes puzzling, such as Stripe's Link wallet or a processor seeking a bank charter.
thesis.how_why: The evidence is each company's own filing or release, read for one point. PayPal's FY2025 10-K separates branded checkout from 'unbranded payments processing' and says Braintree products 'generally have higher expense rates'; it reports lower Braintree volume after a turn to 'profitable growth'. Checkout.com's September 2026 releases report ten acquiring licenses and direct US acquiring under a Georgia limited-purpose bank charter. Block's 10-K describes 'an integrated operating system for local commerce' with custom hardware, and a Utah industrial bank operational since 2021. That the first customer relationship explains what each holds is the author's reading, stated as inference; the companies do not say it, and three cases chosen for contrast cannot prove it. It concerns where a provider's permissions came from, not which customers it can serve now: Stripe and Adyen each sell to the other's first customers. The chapter makes no claim about these companies' internal architecture, because no first-party engineering evidence for them was read, and it does not rank their volumes, which are defined differently (PayPal's TPV, Checkout.com's processed volume, Square's GPV).

role.contribution: Tests the comparison's reading on three companies that started somewhere else, so that the two anchors are seen as two answers among several and the explanation (first customer, then what is owned) is not fitted to two data points.

transition_in.carries_over: Chapter 48's finding that most Stripe and Adyen differences are of default, sequence or degree, traceable to each company's first customers, and that only money-holding and hosting are differences of kind.
transition_in.introduces: Three companies with other first customers (the shopper with a wallet, the enterprise arriving later, the shopkeeper buying a till), each read for the one thing it owns that neither Stripe nor Adyen does.

posts.title: What Is Moving: Agents, Stablecoins and Instant Payments in 2026
posts.question: Which of the changes under way in November 2026 alter how payment infrastructure should be built, and which should an architect only watch?

know: Agent-initiated payments by date and phase: Visa Intelligent Commerce (April 2025), Google's Agent Payments Protocol (September 2025), Stripe and OpenAI's Instant Checkout and Agentic Commerce Protocol (29 September 2025), Stripe's Agentic Commerce Suite (December 2025), Google's Universal Commerce Protocol (January 2026), the Machine Payments Protocol and the x402 Foundation (March and April 2026), Adyen Agentic released in limited availability for US enterprise merchants (June 2026), Stripe Treasury for agents (October 2026); no volume of agent-initiated payments published by either company.

Stablecoins: Stripe's Bridge (completed February 2025), Privy, the Tempo blockchain (mainnet 18 March 2026) and stablecoin balances in preview; Adyen's one published clause on OpenUSD and its place in the digital euro pilot; the US GENIUS Act (approved 18 July 2025, effective 18 January 2027 by the regulator's bulletin) and the EU's MiCA.

Instant account-to-account payments: FedNow's 2025 figures and what their average value suggests, Wero's rollout and the planned migration of iDEAL, Pix and UPI volumes from a secondary source, both companies' pay-by-bank products; the effect on card economics as inference.

PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation: final compromise texts published in April 2026, awaiting the European Parliament's second reading and not in the Official Journal on 17 November 2026, so with no application date yet; and the 2026 consolidation (Global Payments and Worldpay, Stripe and Metronome, Adyen with Orb and Talon.One).
The book's argument in one view: each part answered, for one kind of promise, what to do between the instant answer and the slow truth.
believe: Each change moves or shortens a promise in the payment chain (who authorized the purchase, what the settlement asset is, when the payment is final); none removes the need to know who promised what and to prove that the records agree.
A release phase and a date are part of any statement about these changes; a protocol announced is not a product available.
The answer a payment API returns is still the first of several promises, whoever or whatever asked for the payment.
can_do: Sort a list of proposed projects into build now, prepare and watch, using each change's release phase and the promise it alters.
Judge a new payment technology or provider with three questions before any feature comparison: which promise does it change, who now carries it, and how will I know the money arrived.
Start on their own integration with the payment state card, the idempotency key card and the reconciliation card.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given three proposed projects, the reader sorts them into build now, prepare and wait, citing the release phase or legal status of each from the chapter.
acceptance_criteria.probe: In November 2026 the product lead of a concert-ticketing company proposes three projects for the next quarter: (a) integrate one agent checkout protocol end to end so that AI assistants can buy tickets; (b) hold customer refunds as stablecoin balances; (c) rebuild the customer authentication flows now to meet PSD3 dates. Using only this chapter: which should the team build now, which should it prepare for, and which should it wait on, and why?
acceptance_criteria.expected: (a) Build what every protocol assumes: structured product data, an order-creation endpoint that is idempotent, and seller-of-record logic kept on its own side; do not tie the build to one protocol, because several coexist (ACP, UCP, AP2, the Machine Payments Protocol, x402), Adyen's product was released in limited availability for US enterprise merchants (its product page now says only that it is available in the US) and Stripe says availability varies by integration; neither company has published agent payment volumes. (b) Wait: Stripe's stablecoin balances are in public preview in the United States and private preview elsewhere, the US law takes effect on 18 January 2027, and Adyen has published one clause; if tried, keep such balances behind the same ledger abstractions as other balances so the product can be switched off. (c) Wait for the text: the final compromise texts were published in April 2026 but on 17 November 2026 both files were awaiting the European Parliament's second reading and neither text was in the Official Journal, and the forecasts read give 21 months for application (27 for verification of payee); do not build to dates that are not yet law.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The closing synthesizes the parts as answers to one question about promises, returns to Mila Janssen's €120 class pass (successful at 19:42 on Tuesday 9 March 2027, paid to the studio on Thursday, still reversible in June), and ends on the three toolkit cards; it does not only summarize trends or hand off to the reference pages.
Given a vendor claim the chapter does not contain, the reader applies the book's closing questions to it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A vendor pitches: 'Our network settles every payment in real time, so chargebacks and reconciliation disappear.' Using only this chapter: which questions should you ask before comparing features, and what answers would you expect?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Which promise does it change: finality arrives in seconds instead of days, so the settlement promise is shortened. Who now carries it: a payment that cannot be recalled moves the cost of fraud and of a wrong payment from the issuer's dispute process to the payer and to the merchant's own refund process; the risk is moved, not removed. How will I know the money arrived: the merchant still has two records of the same money, the provider's or network's and its own, and a refund is a new outbound payment with its own state, so reconciliation remains. The instant answer and the truth are closer together; knowing who promised what and proving the records agree is still the work.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone can predict the changes the chapter covers, how each is labeled, and that the chapter closes the book.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: which changes will this chapter examine, in what order, how is each labeled, and how does the chapter end?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Agent-initiated payments and delegated payment authority; stablecoin acceptance and settlement; instant account-to-account payments and card economics; PSD3 and the Payment Services Regulation; consolidation. Each item dated and labeled announced, preview, limited availability or generally available, with both companies' positions; then what to build now and what to watch; then the book's closing, which returns to Mila's class pass.

thesis.question: Which of the changes under way in November 2026 alter how payment infrastructure should be built, and which should an architect only watch?
thesis.claim: Agent-initiated payments, stablecoins and instant account-to-account payments as announced and previewed in November 2026, would each move or shorten one promise in the payment chain (who authorized the purchase, what the settlement asset is, when the payment is final), and none removes the need to know who promised what and to prove that the records agree. An architect should therefore build now only what every variant assumes (a checkout a machine can call, with idempotent order creation; every balance behind one ledger abstraction; a payment state machine whose rules for finality and reversal are set per payment method) and should watch, not build to, anything tied to one agent protocol, one blockchain or a regulatory date not yet published.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that these changes make the existing architecture obsolete: that agents will replace checkout, stablecoins will replace card settlement and instant payments will end chargebacks, so a team should rebuild around whichever arrives first; and the opposite view, that all three are vendor announcements an acquirer-side builder can ignore.
thesis.so_what: The reader leaves the book with a test instead of a forecast: for any new payment technology or provider, ask which promise it changes, who now carries it and how you will know the money arrived. A team applies it by keeping its state machine, keys, ledger and reconciliation, and adding new rails behind them. Mila's €120 was successful on Tuesday, paid out on Thursday and reversible in June; a new rail changes those intervals and who is exposed during them, not the need to track them.
thesis.how_why: The record in November 2026 is mostly announcements and previews with dates. On agents, several protocols coexist (ACP from Stripe and OpenAI in September 2025, Google's AP2 and UCP, the Machine Payments Protocol, x402); Adyen's product was released in limited availability and Stripe's documentation says availability and launch stage 'vary by integration'; neither has published a volume. As published, each of these protocols still ends in an authorization by someone on behalf of someone, which is the promise the book started with. On stablecoins the two companies differ most: Stripe owns an orchestration company, a wallet company, helped start a blockchain and offers balances in preview, while Adyen has published one clause. On instant payments, FedNow's 2025 average payment of about $101,000 points to business transfers, not checkout, and the effect on card economics is inference. PSD3 and the PSR were agreed and not confirmed as published. Each company responds from its starting point (Stripe co-authors protocols and sells a suite that connects a business to several agents; Adyen joins the foundations and implements several), which is the part's argument seen in motion; why Adyen has said so little on stablecoins is not public. Since nothing here is final, the chapter's advice is limited to what the variants share: every agent protocol read calls a merchant's catalog and creates an order from software, which needs structured product data and an order endpoint that tolerates a repeated call; a stablecoin balance is one more balance, which a ledger that already separates balances by type can hold and remove; and an instant payment, a card payment and a direct debit become final at different moments, which the state machine must know per method.

role.contribution: Shows the two companies' positions in motion on the same dated evidence, so the part ends on direction instead of a snapshot, and carries both the part's closing and the journal's closing, returning to Mila's class pass.

transition_in.carries_over: The positions as chapters 46 to 49 fixed them in November 2026: two anchors that started at different ends and are converging, and three other companies that show the starting customer explains what a provider owns.
transition_in.introduces: What is changing under all of them as the book goes to press (agents that pay, stablecoin settlement, instant account-to-account rails, new EU rules, consolidation), each with its date and release phase, and then the question the whole book has been answering.

know: Where each lookup lives: which chapter covers a capability and what the book covers briefly, leaves out or added (domain coverage); the card for a recurring question (toolkit); a term's meaning, its owning chapter and its Stripe and Adyen names (glossary); the dated source behind a claim and the pages citing it (bibliography).
That the planning model behind the coverage map is a model and never a source for a fact about Stripe, Adyen or any other company.
believe: A disagreement between a chapter and a reference page is a defect to fix in one of them, because each reference page is drawn from the chapters.
A claim about a provider is as strong as the kind and the age of the source its bibliography entry names.
can_do: Go from a capability, a question, a term or a claim met in any chapter to the page and row that answers it, without rereading the chapter.
Translate a term between Stripe's and Adyen's documentation, or learn that the two have no one-to-one match.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Every supporting claim of the part thesis is served by at least one reference page, and every page serves at least one.
Each page's closing hand-off names the next reference page, as its successor's transition_in declares.

Where does each answer sit, and what is it?
