Bibliography: one entry with a stable R-number for Adyen's webhook documentation, typed as official documentation, undated ('n.d., accessed 2026-11'), listed under the pages that cite it.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader can say what kind of material each of the four pages is built from and which of it counts as evidence about a company.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only the four reference pages: which of these may be cited for a fact about how Adyen works: the Productscape model named on the coverage page, a filled toolkit card, a glossary definition, a bibliography entry?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Only the source a bibliography entry names, read with its type and date. The Productscape model is a planning map and not a description of any company; the toolkit cards are filled with fictional Larkfield facts; a glossary definition is the book's wording and points to the chapter and source behind it.

thesis.question: Where does a reader look up the book's coverage, templates, terms and sources, and what makes an answer found there reliable enough to act on without rereading the chapter?
thesis.claim: A reference page can be acted on without rereading the chapter when it is generated from the chapters and states its own limit, and each of the four pages does both: the coverage map sends a capability to its chapter and states that its planning model is evidence about no company; the toolkit turns sixteen recurring questions into cards and states that their filled examples are Larkfield's fiction; the glossary gives each term one meaning, an owning chapter and its Stripe and Adyen names, and states where the two providers' terms do not match one to one; the bibliography traces each cited claim to one dated, typed source and states that a source supports no more than its type and date allow.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that reference pages are optional back matter: a reader searches the chapter, the provider's documentation or the web for a term or a source, templates belong in a team's own tools, a vocabulary crosswalk is unnecessary because both providers use the industry's words, and a coverage map only records the author's planning.
thesis.so_what: A reader who meets a term, a card, a capability or a claim in one chapter looks it up in one place and follows the link to its owning chapter or its source; a writer or an AI tool that finds a chapter and a reference page disagreeing treats that as a defect to fix, and neither cites the planning model or a Larkfield figure as a fact about a provider.
thesis.how_why: Each page is produced from the chapters and not written beside them: the coverage rows are checked against the written chapters, each card's fields come from the chapter that teaches it, the glossary's definitions follow the owning chapters, and the bibliography is generated from every page's Sources and Evidence section with stable R-numbers. The crosswalk is needed because the two providers name things differently and sometimes divide them differently: Stripe documents one Account object for a seller where Adyen documents a legal entity, an account holder, a balance account and a transfer instrument, so a word-for-word translation would mislead.

supporting_claims.claim: The coverage map tells a reader which chapter covers each capability of the planning model, which capabilities the book covers briefly or leaves out and why, which subjects the book added, and that the model is a planning map, not evidence about any company.

The toolkit gives each of sixteen recurring questions a card that names the record that counts as the truth, an owner for the exception and a date or deadline, filled once with Larkfield's facts and linked to the chapter that teaches it.

The glossary gives each term the book uses one plain definition beside the terms it is confused with, a link to its owning chapter, and, where the two providers name or divide the thing differently, both names with the difference stated.

The bibliography lists every cited source once with a stable R-number, its date, its evidence type and its citing pages, so a claim can be traced by topic or by chapter and weighed by the age of its source.

role.contribution: Apparatus: coverage map, toolkit, glossary with a Stripe and Adyen vocabulary crosswalk, and bibliography. It argues for no journal claim; it lets the claims be looked up and checked.

flow.rationale: The pages run from the widest lookup to the narrowest: which chapter covers a subject, which record a decision needs, what a word means, which source backs a sentence. No page must be read before another, so the order is a list by design and serves the reader who arrives with a broad question and narrows it; that is why two of the three transitions are plain sequence. The one dependency is that the toolkit's cards use terms the glossary defines, so the glossary follows the toolkit. Putting the bibliography first would open the apparatus with several hundred source entries before the reader has the chapter map that tells them which entries matter to them, and putting the glossary first would separate the book's last chapter, which sends the reader to three cards, from the toolkit by two pages.

hook.content: The planning model behind this book, last reviewed on 15 November 2026, lists 29 capabilities of payments and revenue infrastructure in four groups. None of the 29 is named for card clearing, a card vault, 3-D Secure, idempotency or API versioning, and this book gives each of those a chapter.

opening.bridge: From the chapters, which introduce cards, terms and sources where the argument needs them, to the same material gathered for lookup, starting with the difference between what the plan listed and what the book ended up covering.
opening.roadmap: Domain coverage (capability to chapter, what is covered briefly or left out, what the book added); toolkit (sixteen cards with filled examples); glossary (terms by part, the Stripe and Adyen vocabulary crosswalk, Larkfield names, an alphabetical index); bibliography (sources by topic and by chapter).

closing.synthesis: The four pages answer the four lookups a chapter leaves the reader with (where, which record, what word, what source), and each answer points back to the chapter that owns it. Together they also draw the book's outer line: a planning model that is not evidence, cards filled with fiction, definitions that defer to chapters, and a register in which a claim about a provider ends at a dated document or does not appear.
closing.so_what: A claim, a term or a card in any chapter can be checked against its owning chapter and its dated source without rereading the book, and a disagreement between them is a defect to fix.
closing.callback: The coverage page's opening: a plan of 29 capabilities that had no entry for clearing, vaults or idempotency. The register shows where those chapters' claims came from instead: dated public sources, each listed once.

takeaway.content: Before relying on a statement about Stripe or Adyen from this book, find its source in the register, check the source's type and date, and keep documented facts, labeled inferences and Larkfield apart.

transition_in.carries_over: The cards, terms and sources introduced chapter by chapter, and the last chapter's advice to start with the payment state card, the idempotency key card and the reconciliation card.
transition_in.introduces: The same material gathered for lookup: coverage by capability, the sixteen cards, the vocabulary with its Stripe and Adyen crosswalk, and the register of sources.

posts.title: Domain Coverage
posts.question: Which planning model stands behind the book, which chapters cover its capabilities, and what did the book cover briefly, leave out or add?

know: Which chapter covers each of the 29 capability bricks of the Productscape model of payments and revenue infrastructure, in its four groups: merchant payments, revenue automation, platform money movement, shared financial foundations.

Which capabilities the book covers only briefly (for example hosted checkout and payment links as products, identity verification as a standalone product, delegated authority for agents) or leaves to sibling books, and why.

What the book added that the model has no brick for: how a card payment clears and settles, payment economics, acquiring and licenses, tokenization and PCI scope, authentication, idempotency, API versioning, the whole of Part VIII on scale, the journeys, the failure patterns and the company cases.

That the model is the author's planning map, built with Stripe as the modeled product and Adyen as the comparison, with logical records inferred from modeled jobs: never a source for a fact about either company.
can_do: Find the chapter for a system they own by the job it does.
Say whether a subject is absent from the book by decision or covered under another name.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader finds the chapter that covers a capability, or learns that it is covered briefly or left out and why.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: where does the book cover usage metering and rating, how much does it say about payment links, and does it explain how to post provider payouts into an ERP's general ledger?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Usage metering and rating has its own chapter, usage-metering-and-rating, in Part VI. Payment links are covered briefly, as one of the hosted integration surfaces, not as a product with its own chapter. Posting payouts into the ERP is left out by decision: it is the finance side, covered by the sibling book RECONCILED, and this page links there.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader says what the planning model is, why it is not evidence, and what the book covers that the model does not.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: what is the model behind the book's planning, may a claim about Stripe's internal systems be sourced to it, and name three subjects the book gives a chapter to that the model has no capability for?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A Productscape domain model the author maintains, reviewed on 15 November 2026, of payments and revenue infrastructure with 29 capability bricks; it models products and jobs and does not describe any company's internal services, databases or regions, so no: it is a planning map and is never cited as a source. Any three of: clearing and settlement, payment economics, acquiring and licenses, tokenization and PCI scope, network tokens, 3-D Secure and SCA, idempotency, API versioning, reliability, data stores, multi-region operation, peak load, safe change, the four journeys, the failure patterns, the Stripe and Adyen cases.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict what the page contains and the kind of material it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this page give you, in what order, and from what kind of material?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Tables showing which chapter covers each capability of the planning model, group by group; then what the book covers briefly or leaves out and where to go instead; then what the book added that the model lacks. Material: the planning model and the written chapters, with the model stated not to be evidence about any company.

thesis.question: Which planning model stands behind the book, which chapters cover its capabilities, and what did the book cover briefly, leave out or add?
thesis.claim: The book was planned against a 29-capability Productscape model of payments and revenue infrastructure and gives every capability group at least one chapter, but it is organized differently from the model. It treats product-shaped capabilities (hosted checkout, payment links, standalone identity verification, delegated authority for agents) briefly, inside chapters about the mechanism beneath them; it leaves the finance-side posting of payouts to the sibling book RECONCILED; and it adds what the model has no capability for: how money moves between the parties, the mechanisms that make a retried or changed API call safe (idempotency, versioning, tokenization, authentication) and how the whole is run at scale. The model is a planning map and is evidence about no company.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a book planned from a capability model should follow that model chapter for chapter, so that a mismatch between the two is a gap in the book, and that a detailed model of Stripe's and Adyen's products can be cited for how those companies work.
thesis.so_what: A reader who owns a system finds its chapter by the job the system does, reads an absence as either a stated decision or a different name, and never quotes the model, or this page, for a fact about a provider.
thesis.how_why: A product model answers what a customer can buy and which job it does; an engineer new to payments first needs what happens to the money and why the obvious integration fails, which no product brick states. So Parts I, IV and VIII have few or no bricks behind them, while product-shaped bricks such as hosted checkout or payment links fold into chapters about the mechanism beneath them. The model's own description says it does not attempt to describe either company's internal service topology, physical databases or cloud regions, which is why it can guide coverage and cannot support a claim.

role.contribution: Opens the reference part and sends a reader from a capability to its chapter, saying plainly what is covered briefly, left out or added, and that the planning model is not evidence.

posts.title: Toolkit
posts.question: Which cards and templates do the chapters introduce, and what do the sixteen have in common that makes filling them worth a team's time?

know: The sixteen cards and templates: payment state card, idempotency key card, webhook consumer contract, provider comparison card, funds-flow diagram template, reconciliation card, payout exception card, dispute evidence card, PCI scope card, routing rule card, platform liability card, onboarding requirement tracker, billing retry schedule card, peak plan, provider exit plan card and architecture decision record; the question each answers and the chapter that teaches it.
That every card asks for the same three things: the record that counts as the truth, an owner for the exception, and a date or deadline.
That the filled examples use Larkfield's fictional facts and are to be replaced, and that the provider comparison card is filled only from dated sources or 'Not public'.
can_do: Pick the card for the question on their desk, copy its fields and fill it with their own facts.
Start with the three cards the book's last chapter names (payment state, idempotency key, reconciliation) and say what each must contain for one money-moving call of their own.
Keep the cards current: review on a calendar, let incidents add fields, drop fields nobody reads.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a question from their own work, the reader picks the card that answers it and the chapter that teaches it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: a nightly job that pays out to sellers sometimes times out and is re-run by hand, and last month 30 payouts came back from the receiving banks without anyone noticing for two weeks. Which two cards do you fill in first, which chapters teach them, and which three things does every card ask for?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The idempotency key card (idempotency-and-retries), for what key the payout call sends so that a re-run cannot pay twice; and the payout exception card (payouts-and-money-movement), for who is told when a payout is returned and by when it is resolved. Every card names the record that counts as the truth, an owner for the exception and a date or deadline.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader fills the idempotency key card correctly for a case the page does not contain.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: fill the idempotency key card for 'refund order 8841 in full' in a shop that lets support agents click Refund more than once. What is the key built from, what must it not be built from, and what do you do when the first call times out?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The key is derived from the business event, here the order and the refund's identity (order 8841, full refund, or the refund request's own id), so that every attempt for the same refund sends the same key. It is not a random value generated per attempt or per click. After a timeout the outcome is unknown: fetch the provider's record or retry with the same key; never send a new key.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict what the page contains and the kind of material it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this page give you, in what order, and from what kind of material?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Sixteen cards, from a payment state card to a provider exit plan and an architecture decision record, each with the question it answers, its fields, a filled example and a link to the chapter that teaches it; the three things every card asks for (the record that is the truth, an owner, a date); which three to start with. Material: fictional Larkfield facts in the examples, to be replaced with the reader's own.

thesis.question: Which cards and templates do the chapters introduce, and what do the sixteen have in common that makes filling them worth a team's time?
thesis.claim: A team that cannot write down, for a recurring payment question, the record that counts as the truth, an owner for the exception and a date or deadline has not yet decided that question, and the toolkit's sixteen cards force the decision before an incident does. Each card is introduced by the chapter that raises its question, from the payment state card ('what state is this payment in') through the idempotency key card, the webhook consumer contract and the reconciliation card to the provider exit plan card ('how would we leave this provider'), and each asks for those same three things.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a payment integration is already documented by its code, its provider dashboard and the provider's documentation, so that separate cards duplicate them and go stale, and that what a team left undecided is cheaper to learn from its first incident than to write down in advance.
thesis.so_what: A team fills three cards (payment state, idempotency key, reconciliation) for its own integration before its next release, and treats a blank owner or a blank deadline on any card as work to do now, not as a detail to settle after an incident.
thesis.how_why: Code and dashboards record what a system does when the answer arrives; they do not record who acts when it does not, and that is the case the book's failure patterns come from. Each card is the smallest form that forces the missing decision into writing. At Larkfield no document said what key a renewal retry must send, which system's record of a membership payment was the truth, or who owned a returned payout; the Double Charge, the Silent Webhook and the Payout That Bounced were found by members and studios first.

role.contribution: Gives the part the working records: one card per recurring question, so a decision taught in a chapter can be recorded without rereading it, and gives the book's closing takeaway its destination.

transition_in.carries_over: The coverage page's map from capability to chapter and its closing pointer to the practical records those chapters introduce.
transition_in.introduces: The sixteen cards and templates, each with its question, its fields, a filled Larkfield example and its teaching chapter.

posts.title: Glossary
posts.question: What does each payments, banking and billing term used in the book mean, and what do Stripe and Adyen each call it?

know: The book's terms in one or two plain sentences each, grouped by part, with the chapter that owns each term, dated as of November 2026.
The Stripe and Adyen vocabulary crosswalk: for each concept the book names neutrally, the word each provider's documentation uses, and a note where the two do not divide the concept the same way.
The Larkfield names (people, systems named by role, incidents, Keel decisions K1 to K8) in their own table, marked fictional, and an alphabetical index.
believe: The same word can mean different things at the two providers, and a different word can mean the same thing, so a term is translated by its definition, not by its spelling.
can_do: Look up a term met in a chapter, read it beside the terms it is confused with, and follow the link to the chapter that owns it.
Read a page of one provider's documentation with the other provider's vocabulary in mind, and say where no one-to-one translation exists.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader finds the definition of a contrasted term pair and the chapters that own it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: what is the difference between authorization and settlement, which chapters own the two terms, and why is 'authorized' not 'paid'?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Authorization is the approval by the issuer (the customer's bank) that reserves the amount: a promise, with an expiry. Settlement is the later movement of money between the banks through the network. An authorized payment has moved no money and can still expire, be reversed or fail to be captured. Owning chapters: payment-authorization and clearing-and-settlement.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader uses the crosswalk to translate between the two providers' vocabularies and learns where there is no one-to-one match.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: Stripe's documentation speaks of a 'connected account'; Adyen's speaks of an 'account holder' and a 'balance account'. Are these the same thing? And what does Adyen mean by a 'modification'?
acceptance_criteria.expected: No one-to-one match. For a seller on a platform, Stripe documents one Account object that carries identity, capabilities, requirements and, through its balance, funds; Adyen documents separate resources: a legal entity (who the seller is), an account holder (what the seller may do), a balance account (the seller's money) and a transfer instrument (the seller's bank account). A modification is Adyen's word for any operation on an existing payment (capture, cancel, refund, reversal, amount update), sent as a separate asynchronous request with its own reference. The entries link to platform-payment-models and payment-state-machines.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of a late chapter finds the meaning of a Larkfield name and a Keel decision it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: a chapter in Part VIII mentions 'the Renewal Wave' and 'K5'. What does each mean, and are they facts about a real company?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The Renewal Wave: 38% of Larkfield's monthly membership volume is attempted in a 6-hour window on the 1st; on 1 October 2026 the renewal job hit the provider's rate limit and 7,900 renewals were delayed to the next day. K5: renewals are spread and rate-limited by Larkfield, not by the provider; the job paces itself over 18 hours and retries on a schedule tied to decline codes. Both are fictional: Larkfield is the book's invented platform.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict what the page contains and the kind of material it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this page give you, in what order, and from what kind of material?
acceptance_criteria.expected: One definition per term with a link to the chapter that owns it, grouped by part; then a crosswalk of Stripe's and Adyen's words for the same concepts, with notes where they do not match one to one; then the fictional Larkfield names; then an alphabetical index. Material: the chapters' own definitions and the two providers' documentation as read in November 2026; Larkfield is fictional and legal entries defer to the cited source.

thesis.question: What does each payments, banking and billing term used in the book mean, and what do Stripe and Adyen each call it?
thesis.claim: Stripe and Adyen often use different words for one concept and sometimes divide a concept differently, so a reader moving between the two providers' documentation has to translate by definition, and for some terms, such as the unit that represents a seller on a platform, no one-to-one translation exists. The glossary therefore gives each term one definition in the book's own neutral wording and one owning chapter, and sets beside it, in a crosswalk, the word each provider uses and a note where the two do not match.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that payments has one industry vocabulary that both providers follow, so that a term learned from one provider's documentation carries over to the other and a glossary only repeats what each chapter already defines.
thesis.so_what: A team that integrates both providers, as Larkfield does, defines its own neutral terms from this page and maps each provider's words onto them, instead of letting whichever provider it integrated first name its database columns and its states.
thesis.how_why: Each provider's vocabulary follows its own object model. Stripe exposes a seller as one Account object; Adyen separates the legal entity, the account holder, the balance account and the transfer instrument. Adyen calls a capture, a cancel and a refund modifications, each a separate asynchronous request with its own reference; Stripe speaks of disputes for cards and bank debits alike where Adyen speaks of chargebacks, unpaid direct debits included. A term-by-term table makes these differences visible in one place, and the chapters cited in each row carry the dated documentation behind them.

role.contribution: Gives the book one vocabulary: each term's meaning, its confusable neighbors, its owning chapter and its Stripe and Adyen names, so a chapter can be read out of order and either provider's documentation can be read with the other's in mind.

transition_in.carries_over: The toolkit's cards, whose fields use terms such as idempotency key, clearing account, payout return and PCI scope without defining them.
transition_in.introduces: Every term the book uses, defined and linked to its owning chapter, with the Stripe and Adyen word for each.

posts.title: Bibliography
posts.question: Which sources does the book cite, and how much does each kind of source support?

know: Every public source the pages cite, listed once with a stable R-number, its publication date or 'n.d., accessed 2026-11', its evidence type, the claim it supports and the pages citing it, by topic and by chapter.

The three groups of source the chapters use (company, product and investor sources; standards, regulation and official documentation; research and practitioner sources) and the marks '(secondary source)' and '(evidence age: N years)'.
That the register is generated from the chapters' Sources and Evidence sections, so an R-number identifies a source and does not rank it.
believe: A claim is as trustworthy as the kind and age of its source: a regulation records a requirement, audited accounts record reported numbers, an annual letter what a private company chose to say, documentation an interface as read on a date, an engineering post what a company said it had built that year.
can_do: Trace a figure or a statement in a chapter to its dated source and weigh it by evidence type and date.
Tell from an entry whether a statement about a provider's internals rests on current documentation or on an old engineering post.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader traces a claim to its entry and reads from the entry what kind of evidence it is, how old it is and which pages rely on it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: the idempotency chapter says a Stripe API v1 idempotency key and its stored response are kept for at least 24 hours. Find the entry behind that statement. What kind of source is it, what is its date, and what does the page tell you about how many other pages rely on it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: One entry with an R-number for Stripe's API reference on idempotent requests; official product documentation; undated, marked 'n.d., accessed 2026-11', so the access month says when it was read; the entry lists the pages that cite it, idempotency-and-retries among them.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader weighs a source by its type and date.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: one entry is a 2017 engineering post marked '(evidence age: 9 years)', one is a documentation page marked 'n.d.', and one is marked '(secondary source)'. How far should a reader trust each for a claim about a provider today, and does any source describe Larkfield?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The 2017 post records what the company said it had built in 2017; the current system may differ, and the citing chapter says whether current documentation confirms it. 'n.d.' means undated documentation, so the access month (November 2026) shows when it was read, and it may have changed since. A secondary source is trade press or analysis, used only to fill a gap and named as such in the sentence that cites it. No source describes Larkfield, which is fictional; labeled inferences, recommendations and assumptions are the author's.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader can say what is deliberately absent from the register.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this page: is the Productscape planning model listed as a source for any claim, and where would you find the source for a statement the book marks 'Not public'?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The planning model is named once as planning material and supports no claim. A 'Not public' statement has no source by definition: it records that the public record searched up to the research cut-off of 17 November 2026 does not say.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first section heading) can predict what the page contains and the kind of material it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this page give you, in what order, and from what kind of material?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A register that traces each claim to its source and shows when that evidence was published or read, researched up to 17 November 2026, with 'n.d.' meaning undated; then how to read an entry (R-numbers identify and do not rank; evidence type; evidence age; secondary sources), a topic index, entries by topic and sources by chapter. Material: the chapters' own Sources and Evidence sections; the planning model is listed once as planning material, not evidence, and Larkfield has no sources.

thesis.question: Which sources does the book cite, and how much does each kind of source support?
thesis.claim: The book cites each public source once, under a stable R-number, with its date, its evidence type and the pages that rely on it, and the type and date decide how much the source supports: a regulation or a network rule supports a requirement, audited accounts support a reported figure, undated documentation supports an interface as read in November 2026, and an engineering post supports only what the company said it had built in the year of the post.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that a company's engineering blog is the best evidence of how its systems work regardless of when the post was written, so that a link in the chapter is enough and a register of types and dates adds nothing.
thesis.so_what: A reader who wants to rely on a statement about Stripe or Adyen looks up its entry first and, where the entry is an engineering post older than about three years or an undated page, checks the current documentation before building on it.
thesis.how_why: The register is generated from the chapters' Sources and Evidence sections, so it shows what the chapters do not show one at a time: how many pages lean on one source, and how old the evidence under a subject is. That matters in this book because the public material is uneven: Stripe's best-known posts on idempotency, rate limiting and versioning are from 2017, Adyen's account of its accounting design is from 2021, most documentation pages are undated, and Stripe's company figures come from annual letters while Adyen's come from audited reports.

role.contribution: Closes the book's apparatus: every cited source once, typed and dated, so any claim can be traced to a document by topic or by chapter and weighed by its age.

transition_in.carries_over: The glossary's definitions and crosswalk rows, each of which rests on a chapter and, through it, on a provider's documentation read on a date.
transition_in.introduces: The register of every cited source by topic and by chapter, with its date, evidence type and citing pages.
